title: Your first session
summary: Go from an installed Gravewright to a shared scene with characters, notes and dice.
text: Choose your role Gravewright is a self-hosted virtual tabletop played in a browser. One person operates the installation; campaign game masters prepare the adventure; players join campaigns. These responsibilities are related but have different permissions. Version 0.3.3 is an alpha preview: plan a short rehearsal before relying on a new feature during play. If someone already hosts your game, ask for its address and invitation code. You do not need another server installation to join. Prepare your first game 1. The host follows Installation (wiki:installation), starts the generated Runner and opens the supplied address. On a new installation, create the first owner at /setup . 2. The owner creates a campaign in the campaign library. Choose the native PDF system or a compatible installed system for the sheets you intend to use. 3. Open the tabletop. Create or upload a scene, configure its grid and prepare it privately. 4. Create actors, attach or configure their sheets, assign player access and place their tokens. 5. Add a journal or handout. Check which content each player can read. 6. Invite a player with a campaign code. Use a separate player session to verify the result. 7. Choose Activate for players on the prepared scene. Send a chat message and try 1d20 + 3 in the dice interface. Check the result Both sessions should show the intended broadcast scene. The player should control their character and see only shared material. Opening a private scene as GM does not broadcast it. Saving a Map Builder project does not generate or broadcast a scene. If something is missing Check campaign membership, document permissions and the broadcast scene before reuploading content. For an empty canvas, confirm that the browser supports WebGL and inspect network errors. Reconnecting or refreshing reloads the state authorized for that account. Keep a backup of the installation before significant imports or updates.

title: Install and start Gravewright
summary: Prepare a portable installation on Windows, Linux or macOS and understand what the Runner does.
text: Before you begin Download the complete official release ZIP and extract it to a writable folder. Preserve the folder structure. The installer prepares dependencies and configuration; the generated Runner starts an installation that has already been prepared. Missing tools and packages require internet for their first download. Platform Installer Start after installation --- --- --- Windows x64 Install Windows.bat Gravewright Runner.bat Linux x64 / ARM64 bash "./Install Linux.sh" Gravewright Runner.sh macOS Intel / Apple Silicon Install macOS.command Gravewright Runner.command Windows requires Windows 10 version 1803 or newer, or Windows 11. macOS requires 13.5 or newer. Managed Linux downloads target glibc distributions. Intel Macs also need Apple Command Line Tools and the SDK; the initial cryptography build may take longer. Install and launch 1. Run the installer for your platform from the extracted installation and answer its configuration prompts. 2. Start the generated Runner. Keep its terminal open while playing. 3. Open the address shown; the usual local address is http://127.0.0.1:3000 . 4. Create the owner at /setup , then enter the campaign library. 5. Press Ctrl+C in the Runner terminal when you want to stop the server. Find your files Defaults stay inside this installation: configuration and secrets in .env , database in data/gravewright.sqlite3 , uploads and packages in data/media/ , logs in data/logs/ , tools and caches in data/runner/ . Keep these together when backing up. Two extracted installations have independent state. Recover from startup problems If the Runner says prepared tools are missing, rerun the installer in the complete folder. Rerun it after moving or updating the installation. On Linux/macOS, use bash with the quoted script name if double-click launch fails. A permission failure needs the reported folder made writable; do not move only the database as a workaround. The generated Runner serves the local computer on loopback. Remote players need an intentionally configured public host with HTTPS and WebSockets; see the developer deployment reference. A running local address alone does not make your table reachable over the internet.

title: Campaigns, invitations and players
summary: Create a campaign, invite people and distinguish player accounts from spectator links.
text: Create the campaign The installation owner creates campaigns in the campaign library at /inside . Choose a meaningful name, cover and system appropriate to your sheets. Open the campaign to prepare its tabletop. A campaign keeps its own membership and resources; joining one does not grant access to another. The built-in Gravewright PDF System is a general sheet foundation. Other RPG systems are installed separately. Confirm compatibility before building a campaign around an optional package. Choose or change the cover 1. Open campaign creation or editing in the library. Fill in the campaign fields and choose the cover source: From computer or By URL . Local images support PNG, JPEG or WebP, up to 5 MB. 2. For a local image, drag it onto the upload area or focus the file control and activate it with the keyboard. The operating system's file picker still opens when choosing a file. For a URL, use the URL field instead. 3. Inspect the preview before saving. Remove image clears a newly selected image or an existing saved cover. Selecting the already active source again keeps the current image; changing the source clears that selection so you can choose its replacement. 4. Save the form and check the campaign card. If validation fails, correct the indicated field and submit again. Campaign dialogs and the other host forms use the same themed fields, upload controls, focus and error states. On a narrow screen, scroll within the modal to reach its actions. Actor and folder creation also use application modals: Cancel closes without creating the resource, and controls pause while saving. Keep the form open until success or a useful error appears. Invite a player 1. Ask the player to register at /register , or log in at /login if they already have an account. 2. As campaign GM, create an access code and choose its validity and maximum uses. 3. Give the player the host address and the code through your usual private channel. 4. Have them join the campaign, then check their membership and assign the appropriate actor and document access. 5. Revoke the code when it is no longer needed. Successful entry by a new member increments the code's use count. If joining fails, check expiration, revocation, remaining uses and the campaign associated with the code. An account on the server does not automatically become a member of every campaign. Prepare for the session Choose Manage campaign on the campaign card to prepare its native documents, sheets and planning tools without entering the table. The campaign manager (wiki:campaign-management) is available to campaign GMs, including co-GMs; it does not broadcast a scene or create table presence. Use folders and clear names for scenes, actors and journals. Prepare private scenes without broadcasting them; activate the intended scene when the group is ready. If lobby/readiness controls are enabled, use them to coordinate the start. Use spectator access deliberately A streamer link is restricted read-only access. It does not replace a player account and cannot edit the campaign or its Map Builder projects. Test what the spectator actually sees before broadcasting; private GM preparation and player document permissions still need deliberate configuration. To troubleshoot a missing actor or journal, check resource access after confirming membership. To troubleshoot a missing map, check scene visibility and the current broadcast. See Permissions (wiki:permissions) for a practical rehearsal.

title: Manage a campaign before play
summary: Prepare the same campaign records outside the table, with seven GM planning and recovery tools.
text: Open the GM workspace Choose Manage campaign on the campaign card or its cover preview. Every current campaign GM can enter, including a co-GM with a participant account. Being the installation owner alone does not grant management access to a campaign where that account is only a player. Players and streamers use their authorized tabletop tools instead. The manager and table share the same journals, quests, actors, sheets, items, scenes, library, audio, cards, compendiums, clocks (wiki:clocks), clues (wiki:clues) and mind maps (wiki:mindmaps). Preparing here creates no table presence and changes no scene broadcast. Scene generation, scene updates and live actions retain their own explicit controls. Use the seven preparation tools Tool Practical use --- --- Personal dashboard Pin documents and arrange panels for the next session, pending work, diagnostics and events Session planner Order scenes, encounters, quests, characters, audio and notes; keep a checklist and finish with a summary and pending work Timeline and calendar Record free-text world dates, optional calendar dates, upcoming events and linked documents Quest columns Change status, inspect prerequisites and assigned characters, and mark visible objectives complete Connections Inspect links and usages for characters, items, journals and scenes, including typed journal references View as player Inspect the server-filtered documents of a selected player in a read-only preview History and trash Compare journal revisions, restore a version or recover a deleted journal and its retained files Each GM has a personal dashboard; session plans and timeline records are shared GM preparation. These records are not delivered to players. The manager refreshes authorized state automatically. A conflict requires reviewing the current version; keep the draft open instead of silently replacing another GM's revision. Prepare and verify 1. Select the intended scene context without changing the table's broadcast. 2. Edit the native sheets and journals, prepare progress and link the session's documents. 3. Use View as player to inspect the intended audience, then test interactive actions in a separate player session. 4. Save before leaving the selected editor. Use journal history to compare a change before restoring it. 5. Enter the table and activate a scene only when the group is ready. Campaign copies and exports include selected preparation and journal history; snapshots preserve campaign recovery state. Omitted targets do not acquire unrelated resource identities, and missing retained files prevent an incomplete restore. A campaign ZIP does not replace a consistent installation backup. See the campaign reference (docs:campaign-management) and backup and upgrade steps (wiki:backups-updates).

title: Progress clocks and pinned goals
summary: Share segmented objectives between the table and campaign manager, with explicit audience and progress permissions.
text: Configure a clock Open Clocks from the lower table dock, or choose Manage campaign → Clocks . A GM names the clock, enters an optional description, chooses its color and sets 2–24 segments. Campaign scope follows the campaign across scenes; scene scope appears only with its associated scene. Both interfaces edit the same records. Choose GM only or Players . A public clock may optionally allow players to advance or reduce progress; this grants no configuration, reset or deletion rights. Streamers remain read-only. Pinned clocks show only a name and face on the table. Private clocks and out-of-scope records are filtered before delivery. Advance and inspect When permitted, left-click the clock face to advance one segment or right-click to reduce one. Focus the face and use Right/Up or Left/Down for the same actions. Progress remains bounded and shared; wait for the pending action before repeating it. The full editor also offers progress buttons. Double-click the name, or focus it and press Enter/Space. A GM opens the native editor. Players and streamers open a read-only description modal after a fresh access check. Clock descriptions contain up to 4,000 authored characters and keep their original language. Arrange your local indicators Drag each pinned clock by its title. Arrow keys move a focused title one pixel; Shift moves ten, and Escape cancels a drag. Cards and unfilled segments have transparent backgrounds. Positions are stored only in that browser for the account, campaign and indicator; wide and narrow screens keep separate layouts. A read-only viewer can arrange permitted indicators. Moving sends no position command or broadcast and changes no shared progress. Use MapBuilder's Control clock to bind a Smart Object to a specific GM-authored action. It respects scope and grants no general editing rights. Rehearsal rolls back its effects. Review the clock reference (docs:clocks) for limits, APIs and retries, and clues (wiki:clues) for staged discoveries.

title: Reveal clues through discovery
summary: Prepare a finding privately and reveal it only after its progress is complete and its audience permits sharing.
text: Prepare the discovery Open Clues from the lower table dock or from Manage campaign . As GM, enter a name, player-facing Content , private GM notes , color and 1–24 progress segments. Use one segment for a single discovery or several for an investigation. Choose campaign or scene scope and whether to pin the clue. Players and streamers receive the record only when progress is complete and visibility is Reveal when discovered . Until then, they receive no name, identifier, unfinished progress or undiscovered count. GM notes remain private after revelation. This is the same saved clue in the table and manager, independent of RPG system. Advance, reveal and hide Only GMs change progress directly: left-click the progress bar to advance one step, right-click to reduce, or use its arrow keys. Reveal completes discovery and selects player visibility; Hide selects GM-only visibility without clearing progress; Reset clears progress without changing visibility. Reducing a completed clue hides it again until complete. Players may remember text they have already read. Pinned clues show only a name and progress bar. Double-click the name or press Enter/Space: a GM opens the native editor, while players and streamers read the discovered Content in a simple description modal. Access is checked again; GM notes never become the description. Move and connect the indicator Drag the title to arrange a pinned clue locally; arrows move one pixel and Shift moves ten. Positions stay per account/campaign/browser and retain separate wide/narrow layouts. Transparency and dragging follow the clock controls (wiki:clocks); moving does not broadcast or change shared progress. MapBuilder's Control clue delegates a configured advance, reduction, value, reset, revelation or hiding action through native permission checks. It does not give players a general clue editor. See the clue reference (docs:clues) and Smart Objects (wiki:smart-objects).

title: Collaborative mind maps
summary: Connect campaign topics, grant selected players editing access and link 37 native resource types.
text: Create a graph Open Mind maps in the lower table dock or campaign manager. A GM creates a named map, chooses campaign/scene scope and sets visibility and editors. New maps are GM-only. Add root, child or sibling topics, edit notes/color/completion, collapse branches and draw additional labeled connections. Drag topics to position them; drag empty canvas to pan, use zoom or Fit map . Undo/redo affects the local draft. Save mind map sends the expected saved version. A conflict keeps the draft and offers explicit reload; it does not silently overwrite another editor. Closing modified work asks whether to discard it. Grant the intended access All campaign GMs edit maps. Visible to players grants reading, while selected player editors can also read and edit a private map from the table. Those editors may rename the map and edit topics, but cannot change scope, visibility, the editor list or delete the map. Streamers remain read-only. Scene-scoped maps additionally require access to their scene. The campaign manager itself remains GM-only. Topic notes belong to the whole map's audience: keep private planning in a private map. A hidden link does not make the surrounding authored text private. Link campaign resources Use Link campaign resource to search the authorized catalog of 37 native types: characters and files, items, journals/pages/quests, scenes and objects, tokens, encounters, clocks, discovered clues, audio, cards, compendiums, preparation, authoring resources, visible chat messages and mind maps. The complete reference (docs:mindmaps) lists the types and availability rules. Links keep typed identities and recheck access on opening. They neither copy documents nor grant permission. Missing and denied targets look equally unavailable, with no private identifier or title. Saving another topic preserves an existing unavailable link through an opaque placeholder; removing it deletes the connection. Integrate and transfer MapBuilder offers Open mind map and Control mind-map topic . Opening rechecks each recipient; completion controls delegate only the configured effect. Native rehearsal rolls back effects and receipts. Campaign copies select Mind maps , remap included typed resources, keep local topic IDs and authored text, and clear source player-editor grants. Snapshots restore the same campaign's grants. A campaign supports 64 maps; a graph supports 500 topics, 1,000 additional connections, 16 links per topic and 2,048 links overall. See the API and graph limits (docs:mindmaps) before building an integration.

title: Permissions and safe sharing
summary: Check exactly what a player can view, edit or control before sharing your preparation.
text: Understand the boundaries The installation owner administers the host. A campaign GM manages that campaign. Players receive access through campaign membership and resource permissions. A streamer remains read-only. Server checks apply to actions and protected files; a URL or a visible button is not an access grant. Actor and journal access use levels such as None , Limited , Read and Owner . The exact limited preview depends on the resource. Read access does not grant editing or token control. Scene access, token ownership, journal page access and GM-only sections are separate decisions. Rehearse sharing 1. Keep your GM session open and sign in as a player in a separate browser profile. 2. Give that player the intended actor permissions. Verify that its sheet opens and that unrelated actors remain protected. 3. Place the actor's token in a visible scene and test movement with the player account. 4. Share one journal and one page intentionally. Include a harmless sample GM secret and confirm it is absent from the player view. 5. Activate the intended scene for players and verify the broadcast. 6. If you use a streamer link, inspect it independently of the player session. Avoid accidental disclosure Editor layer visibility in Map Builder is an editing aid: preview and generation include all project layers. Use the tabletop's GM visibility controls for private scene images. A screenshot, download or export can have a different audience from the live table. Universal VTT omits GM-only images, but secret-door geometry may still be present in its exported file. Review it before sending it to players. Never assume that a campaign export is a player-safe handout. When access looks wrong Check the account, campaign role and explicit permission on the particular resource or page. Confirm that the intended scene is public and broadcast. Reconnect after permissions or memberships change to verify fresh authorized state. Grant the smallest access needed instead of making all documents public to diagnose one missing resource.

title: Navigate and run the tabletop
summary: Find the tools for the current scene and establish a dependable session routine.
text: Find your workspace The tabletop combines the map canvas, tool controls, resource directories and windows for sheets and documents. Available controls depend on your role, the active tool and installed modules. Game masters can prepare privately while players stay on the broadcast scene. The main resource areas are scenes, actors, journals, chat and dice, audio, cards, combat and compendiums. The system provides sheet and rule behavior; browser modules may extend the interface. Start a session 1. Open the campaign and confirm that its required system and modules load. 2. Open the intended scene as GM. Check the grid, walls, lighting and initial camera view. 3. Confirm actor ownership and place the required tokens. 4. Open the journals and reference material you need; share only the intended pages. 5. Activate the scene for players and check a player session. 6. Have players send a message, roll dice and interact with the table before starting the encounter. Work on the map Choose the tool for the operation: selection and movement, drawing, measurement, walls, fog, lighting, pings or effects. A selected token must be controlled and unlocked before it can move. Changing the active tool can explain why a click selects, measures or draws instead of moving a piece. Keep the scene's complexity appropriate for the browsers in your group. WebGL is required for map rendering. Heavy visual effects, large images and many objects can affect clients differently; simplify and compare with a small scene when diagnosing rendering problems. Set your ping color and mouse pointers Open the Gravewright menu → Preferences . Under Map ping , choose your Identification color . Hold on the map to ping; the GM can hold Shift to focus the table's cameras. That saved color also identifies your shared pointer and your dot in the GM's scene list. Under Mouse pointers , choose Show participants' pointers and Share my pointer independently. Hiding other pointers does not stop sharing yours. Disabling sharing immediately hides your pointer for others, while map pings still work. These two preferences are saved for your profile on this device; they do not change another player's settings. Pointers appear only between authorized viewers of the same scene, and a stationary pointer remains visible. Streamers can view pointers but do not publish their own. Map keyboard shortcuts 1. Open the Gravewright menu → Keyboard shortcuts . 2. Choose the field for an available tool or window and press the intended key combination. Escape cancels recording. 3. If a conflict or reserved combination is reported, choose another combination. Tool bindings have their layer's scope; window bindings apply across layers. 4. Use Unassign to remove one binding or Restore defaults to restore the defaults. Mappings stay with your profile on this device. The list covers the table's supported tools and windows; gestures inside individual tools keep their own controls. Shortcuts do not take over normal text entry or modal keyboard navigation. Label a local measurement Open Measurement , choose a line or area shape and drag on the map. Enable Title for the selected marking and type in the field beside its displayed dimensions. For example, label an area Dangerous ground . The text follows that marking alongside its size. Measurements and their titles stay local to this browser session; use a shared scene object or handout when other players need a persistent label. Drawing remains available through Mini Paint; the separate Shapes tool is removed. Reconnect and finish If updates stop, check the network and reconnect. Refreshing reloads authorized server state; it does not turn an unsaved browser draft into a saved project. Keep an interrupted Builder tab open until recovery is complete. At the end, stop audio, confirm important edits have saved and take a campaign snapshot or installation backup when appropriate. The host can stop the Runner with Ctrl+C after the group has left.

title: Scenes, grids and the player broadcast
summary: Prepare a map privately, choose an import method and put the intended scene on screen.
text: Choose how to create the scene Starting material Use Result --- --- --- A plain colored surface New scene → Empty map A native scene with your chosen dimensions and optional grid A finished map image New scene → Upload map A native scene An editable map you want to build New scene → Map Builder An editable project, then a generated scene A finished image to decorate in the Builder Library → Import → Import ready-made map A project background with editable additions A .uvtt, .dd2vtt or .df2vtt file Import Universal VTT A native scene with supported geometry and lighting A normal image upload does not discover walls or reconstruct original layers. Universal VTT imported through the scene directory creates a native scene; imported through Builder it creates a linked scene and editable project. The flattened background remains one image. Prepare and share 1. As campaign GM, create the scene in the intended folder. 2. Configure its name, grid and initial view. Match the cell size and image alignment before placing tokens. 3. Add or inspect walls, doors, fog and lights using the scene tools. 4. Place a test token and check movement and vision with a player account. 5. Choose Activate for players when the scene is ready. This makes it visible and broadcasts it in one operation. Opening a scene privately as GM preserves the players' broadcast. Generating a Builder scene also begins privately; broadcasting remains a separate action. Updating a linked scene changes what clients already viewing that scene receive. Create an empty map Choose Scenes → New scene → Empty map . Enter the scene name, background color, Width (px) and Height (px) . Set Show grid , then choose whether Activate after creation should be enabled. Uncheck activation to prepare privately while the players keep their existing scene. Choose Create map . The new scene uses the current folder and supports the normal scene tools; no background upload is needed. Send selected players to a scene 1. As GM, open the scene's context menu and choose Activate for selected players . 2. Select one or more campaign players and choose Activate . The selected players must have access to that scene; everyone else stays on their current destination. 3. Inspect the identification dots in the scene list. Their colors are each player's saved ping color; hover a dot for the player's name. Offline players retain their assigned destination. 4. To reunite the table, choose Activate for players on the common scene. This clears individual destinations and activates it for everyone. The GM badge shows the scene you are viewing, including a private preview; it does not mean that every player sees it. If one player still sees another map, check their individual destination and scene access before reactivating or uploading anything. Manage generated scenes carefully Scenes linked to a Builder project have a red map icon for the GM and an Edit with MapBuilder action. Reopen the project there and use Update scene to apply changes to the same scene. Compatible manual edits to generated resources are imported when opening the project, returning to its tab and before updating. Scene-only objects stay separate. Changes to different properties can merge; competing edits to the same property pause synchronization and preserve your local draft. Follow Builder synchronization and recovery (wiki:map-builder) before continuing. Troubleshoot If players see the previous map, check the broadcast and the success of scene generation/update. For an upload timeout, inspect the scene directory before uploading again: server processing may have finished after the connection closed. Image byte size, decoded pixels, dimensions and tile counts have separate limits configured by the host. A larger byte allowance does not guarantee that a huge image can be rendered.

title: Actors and your character directory
summary: Organize reusable character documents, grant ownership and place representations in scenes.
text: Actor or token? An actor is a reusable character document in the campaign. A token is its representation in one scene. Sheet data and the token's position or visual state are related but distinct. The campaign system supplies supported actor types and sheet behavior; the native PDF system uses the character type. Prepare a character 1. As GM, open the actor directory and create an actor of a supported type. 2. Give it a clear name and organize it in a folder. Add portrait or token art that you may legally use. 3. Open the sheet. For the native system, attach and configure the character PDF; for an installed system, follow that package's sheet controls. 4. Configure the actor's permissions for the intended player. Ownership grants editing access; read access alone does not. 5. Put a token in the intended scene and confirm its sheet source and appearance. 6. Verify opening, editing and movement in a separate player session. Reuse characters deliberately A linked token reads actor data. A snapshot token keeps an independent copy for that token. This distinction matters when using multiple creatures based on one actor: editing an independent creature should not accidentally change the reusable source. Check the token's link mode before changing resources through its sheet. Folders help organize the directory but do not replace resource permissions. Deleting or changing assets can affect documents that reuse them; inspect references before removing a shared image. Troubleshoot If a player cannot see an actor, confirm campaign membership and the actor's permissions. If the actor opens but cannot be edited, check ownership. If the token sheet differs from the directory actor, inspect whether the token uses a snapshot. If expected sheet fields are absent, verify the campaign's system and its installed version instead of assuming every system has the same schema. The core does not include a universal item catalog or system-specific rules. The native PDF system has no native item types; install a suitable system package when you need those capabilities.

title: Character sheets and the PDF system
summary: Use an existing character PDF or the sheet supplied by an installed RPG system.
text: Choose the right sheet The included Gravewright PDF System lets a campaign use PDF character sheets without making the host depend on a particular RPG. Installed systems can instead provide their own fields, resources, item types, translations and automation. A sheet shown for an optional system is not a promise that its rules are built into the core. Prepare a PDF character 1. Create or open an actor in a campaign using the PDF system. 2. Upload a character-sheet PDF you are authorized to use. 3. Open the sheet's PDF editing/mapping controls and configure the fields needed by your group. 4. Enter a few sample values, save and reopen to confirm persistence before filling the entire character. 5. Grant the intended player ownership and verify the sheet from that player's session. 6. If you reuse the layout, verify it on another character before investing in a larger collection. Mapping fields onto a PDF does not import a rulebook or implement all calculations from an RPG. Agree with your group on which values you maintain manually and which an installed system actually automates. Map a PDF without editable fields As GM, choose Map fields , then text, number, checkbox or multiline text. Drag a rectangle onto the page or choose Add field , name it and adjust its bounds. Drag moves it; its lower-right handle resizes it. Arrow keys move one displayed pixel and Shift moves ten. Choose Finish mapping to fill values. Native PDF widgets and manual overlays use the same authorized sheet values; the source PDF is unchanged, and there is no OCR step. Double-click a native or manual field, or press F2 while it is focused, to configure Field actions . Bind a value to a token bar or choose a saved dice action. Six presets include d20, highest/lowest of two d20s, 2d6, exploding d6 and 4dF. 1d20 + @value reads this field; 1d20 + @{field-key} reads another numeric field. Use Reference field for exact keys. Authorized editors run saved actions with the roll button or Alt+Enter; a GM double-click opens configuration. Dice permissions and normal visibility still apply. Use the authoring and reuse tools Capability What to check --- --- Calculated fields Arithmetic and field references recompute on save; cycles are rejected and calculated values are read-only Layout editing Multiple selection, copy/paste, duplicate, alignment, distribution and optional snapping apply to the active layout Undo and redo Up to 50 local layout steps preserve current character values; changing the PDF clears this history Mapping JSON Transfer layout definitions, bindings, actions and calculations without PDF bytes or character values Mapping library Save a reusable campaign template and apply it to the same PDF layout, with field identities preserved Batch application Apply to selected permitted actors; all target revisions are validated before committing Diagnostics and filled PDF Inspect missing fields/references and layout mismatches; export a separate flattened PDF with current values These tools complement manual mapping and saved actions; they do not automatically supply RPG rules. Filled export is bounded and fails on overflow instead of silently returning an incomplete document. See the PDF System reference (docs:pdf-system) for limits and formulas. Edit the intended source Opening a sheet from a linked token uses actor data; an independent snapshot token uses its own copy. Check this before changing health, notes or other resources on duplicate creatures. A missing portrait or PDF may be an asset-access issue rather than a missing actor. Recover from a save conflict If another session changed the sheet, reload the current state and reapply the intended edit. Do not repeatedly force an old form over a newer revision. If a save response is uncertain after connection loss, inspect the reopened sheet before entering the same change again. Content and limits The native PDF system does not include item types or a proprietary catalog. PDFs and images retain their own licenses; owning a book does not automatically authorize redistributing it in public downloads. Keep licensed personal material in the private campaign storage and share only within your authorization.

title: Tokens, movement and vision
summary: Control a character on the map and understand linked data, collision and visibility.
text: Place and configure 1. As GM, open the intended scene and place a token based on an actor. 2. Check its image, size, name and whether it reads linked actor data or an independent snapshot. 3. Configure visibility, lock and vision settings for the role it will play. 4. Give the player the appropriate actor ownership and test selection and movement in their session. 5. Check walls, doors and lighting from that player's view before starting play. Choose token labels and bars As GM, right-click the token and choose Configure . Set Token name display to always visible, selected, hovered, or selected-or-hovered. Names, initials and condition text stay sharp across map zoom. The fixed decorative gold outline is removed. For Bar 1 and Bar 2 , choose Bar color and Bar visibility independently: Everyone , Owner and GM , or GM only . Bar 1 appears 5px above the token; bar 2 appears 5px below it. The system's sheet supplies the bar values. Restricted bars are filtered before delivery to other viewers; verify the result with a player who does not own that token. These presentation settings add no numerical bar labels. Set Show turn indicator if the current/next-turn outline should appear, then save. Appearance follows duplication without changing the actor's RPG rules or sheet schema. A display preference does not grant control of the token. Move during play Use the selection/movement tool and a token you control. The server verifies permissions, the current revision, scene bounds and wall collision. A token can be visible without being controlled. A controlled token can still be locked or blocked by a wall. Pings and measurement help communicate intended movement, but do not bypass these restrictions. The vision available to the player depends on eligible controlled tokens and scene configuration; the GM's view is not an accurate substitute for a player test. Understand linked and snapshot data A linked token's sheet source is the actor. An independent token's source is its snapshot. Check this when multiple creatures use the same actor and when a resource change appears on one creature but not another. Position, scene state and sheet data do not all have the same source. Diagnose movement and vision Symptom Check --- --- Cannot select or move Active tool, control permissions and token lock Movement stops Walls, closed doors, scene bounds and a refreshed token revision Player sees an empty/dark area Broadcast scene, token visibility, vision enabled/range and lighting A character has unexpected values Linked versus snapshot sheet source Automation fires while crossing an object Its area-entry/exit blueprint and token path Movement through a Smart Object area can trigger both entry and exit when a path crosses the entire area. Configuration changes are different from accepted movement events. Use the GM automation log to investigate rather than disabling ownership or wall checks.

title: Chat and dice notation
summary: Send table messages and learn a useful set of native dice expressions.
text: Send the right message Open chat, check its scene/audience context and send a short test message. Select private or GM delivery only through the supported audience controls, and verify the recipient before sending secrets. A roll result is stored with its message; another user's refresh should not create another roll. Roll an expression Use the dice interface to submit an expression. The native notation uses a lowercase d , positive integer counts and faces, arithmetic and parentheses. Expression Meaning --- --- 1d20 + 3 Roll a d20 and add three 2d6 + 1 Sum two d6 and add one 4d6kh3 Keep the highest three of four d6 2d20kl1 Keep the lower of two d20 1d6! Explode recursively on the maximum face 1d6r1 Reroll a one once 4dF Four Fudge dice 8d10 = 8 Count successful active dice at least eight Modifiers attach directly to their dice term: 4d6kh3 works; separating kh3 with a space does not. Recursive rerolls/explosions are bounded by the engine; an expression can be rejected for complexity. Watch comparison spacing 1d6!=5 means exploding on a five. 1d6 != 5 is an expression comparison. 2d6! =5 is conditional explosion; 2d6! = 5 explodes normally then counts successes. Use spaces deliberately when mixing modifiers and comparisons. Supported numeric functions include floor , ceil , round , abs , min , max and clamp in lowercase. Unknown functions and chained comparisons are rejected. Respond to an object's roll request A GM can configure a Dice challenge or Request dice roll action in a Smart Object (wiki:smart-objects). An authorized recipient receives a native prompt with its expression and label. Review it and press Roll explicitly; receiving the prompt does not roll automatically. The server validates the expression and posts the result to the configured public or GM audience through the normal dice service. Retries and multiple tabs reuse the same logical roll for that recipient. Streamers do not receive actionable requests. The object graph continues after requesting the roll; it does not wait for the result or apply RPG-specific success, damage or rewards. Those rules belong to the chosen system package. Troubleshoot If a roll fails, simplify to 1d20 , then add one modifier at a time. Check lowercase notation and modifier spacing. After a lost connection, inspect chat for the committed result before submitting a new roll. A new submission is a new logical roll, even if its expression is identical. Installed systems may add their own roll controls without changing the meaning of every native expression.

title: Journals, quests and roll tables
summary: Keep campaign knowledge, share handouts and track objectives without exposing GM notes.
text: Choose a document Journals include structured notes, quests, quest boards and weighted roll tables. Use a journal for reference material, a quest for objectives and rewards, a board to organize quests and a roll table for weighted results. Image/PDF attachments let you keep related handouts with the document. Prepare and share a journal 1. Create a document in the journal directory and choose its type. 2. Organize its pages or content sections and add authorized attachments. 3. Put private preparation in GM sections rather than relying on an obscure page title. 4. Set document and page access for the intended people. Read access and editing ownership are distinct. 5. Use the available presentation/handout controls to show the intended material. 6. Check the result as a player; a shared document does not imply every private section becomes public. Organize independent chapters and pages Choose New chapter to create an empty chapter, optionally under another chapter. A chapter can hold pages and subchapters; each page belongs to one chapter or none. Use Move to chapter or No chapter on a page. Deleting a chapter keeps its pages ungrouped and moves its direct subchapters to its parent. Page deletion is a separate action. Protected pages can prevent removal of a required chapter. While editing a page you own, click its header name or focus it and press Enter/Space. Enter or leaving the field confirms its title; Escape cancels, and an empty name keeps the previous title. Content and links remain intact. Collapse pages makes room on narrow screens; Show pages restores the index. The diary supports 128 chapters, eight chapter levels and 64 pages. Older category groupings become stable chapters. Hidden-only branches remain filtered; readable page paths and genuinely empty chapters remain visible. Existing history and campaign copies retain the hierarchy. Insert references with @ In editable rich text, type @ at the start of a paragraph or after a space. Search the authorized campaign catalog, choose a type and select Add link . Confirming replaces the typed marker; cancelling keeps it as ordinary text. An @ inside an email does not open the picker, and / still opens the block menu. The same 37-type catalog used by mind maps (wiki:mindmaps) includes sheets, journals/pages, quests, items, scenes, clocks, discovered clues and other native resources. Opening rechecks target access; a shared journal does not grant access to its links. Unavailable targets reveal no private name or identity. Source-bound opaque placeholders preserve existing hidden references during otherwise authorized edits; guessed private targets cannot be inserted. This works in the table and campaign manager (wiki:campaign-management). See the journal reference (docs:journals) for permissions and transfers. Track a quest Enter the player-facing description, status, objectives, rewards and assigned characters. Keep GM notes separate. Decide which objectives and rewards players should see. Link the quest to a board when you want a grouped view; hidden quest status, explicit denial and actor access still affect what each player sees. For an interactive quest giver, bind a fixed campaign quest in the Smart Object's Quest giver or Quest completion model. The GM-authored Set quest status action changes that quest through the journal service. A player interacting with the object receives only that configured action, not general permission to edit quests. Open journal can present a journal, quest or board to selected recipients, but does not grant read access: configure document permissions first. A behavior playtest reports the planned changes and deliveries without saving quest state or opening player windows. Draw from a weighted table Add active entries with appropriate weights and choose whether results are replaced after drawing. Check the result audience before a draw. A GM-only result is filtered for players even when they can access the table. If no eligible weight remains in a table without replacement, reset or adjust its entries before drawing again. Limits and troubleshooting Quests support up to 64 objectives and 64 rewards, with up to 32 assigned characters. Roll tables support up to 256 entries. If a document appears on a board but cannot be edited, inspect its own access. If an attachment fails, check the file's campaign and permissions rather than publishing its storage URL. Reopen a document after a revision conflict and reapply the intended change to the current version.

title: Music, ambience and positional audio
summary: Prepare reusable tracks and playlists, then check what players actually hear.
text: Prepare your audio The GM manages campaign tracks, playlists and scene playback. Tracks can be music, ambience or effects. Upload only audio you may use, give tracks clear names and test that the browser can play each file. Effect tracks are one-shot rather than looping music. Build a session soundscape 1. Upload and classify your tracks in the audio workspace. 2. Set sensible volume and loop options on each track. 3. Create a playlist, select its tracks and choose sequential, shuffle or repeat playback as appropriate. 4. Open the intended scene and start playback there. Use pause, stop, seek and volume controls as needed. 5. Ask a player to interact with the page and confirm that audio is audible before the session. Playlists support up to 200 tracks. Scene soundscape presets are reusable collections; a track on disk is not automatically playing in every scene. Add positional sound Place a sound source in the scene and configure its radius, gain, falloff and occlusion. Test from the position of a controlled token. Walls and sound barriers can affect attenuation; the GM's listening context can differ from a player's. Smart Objects can play a campaign sound or control a sound already playing in the scene. Troubleshoot silence or uneven playback Browsers often require a click or other interaction before audio starts. Check site/tab mute, system output, volume, scene and playback state first. For positional audio, inspect source enabled state, radius, token position and occlusion. Reconnect to refresh synchronized playback after an interruption. Deleting a campaign track can detach playlist entries, positional sources and blueprint references using it. Stop playback and inspect reuse before removing a shared track. Deleting the file is different from removing one source from one scene; keep originals in your normal content backup.

title: Decks, hands and cards on the table
summary: Create a deck, draw cards and control when their faces become visible.
text: Prepare a deck The GM creates deck definitions and playable deck instances. A definition is a reusable setup; an instance carries the current draw pile, hands and discard state. Use names and front/back images you are authorized to distribute to your group. 1. Open the cards workspace and create the deck with its cards and optional images. 2. Create the playable instance where the workflow offers a reusable definition. 3. Shuffle the draw pile before play if your game needs random order. 4. Draw to a hand, the scene/table or chat using the destination controls. 5. Check the result with a second account before drawing secret information during play. Decks contain 1–500 cards. One draw requests 1–50 cards, and the pile must contain enough eligible cards for the entire request. Manage a hand A hand belongs to its recipient. Its owner can inspect its faces. Cards placed in a scene expose their fronts only when revealed; other viewers receive the concealed representation. A GM may draw for another campaign member. Having access to a deck does not disclose every other person's hand. Owners and the GM can use the supported actions to place, take, flip, move, give, discard or return cards. Watch the destination and face state when moving from a private hand to the public table. Understand chat and reset Cards drawn to chat create a durable message attachment containing public faces only. Later flipping or moving a live card does not retroactively turn that stored public attachment into a secret. Review the audience before using chat for a draw. Shuffle randomizes the remaining draw pile. Reset returns the deck's cards to the draw pile, clears owners and scene positions and hides faces; it changes the whole active deck. Use it between rounds only when everyone agrees the current hands can end. If a draw fails for insufficient cards, inspect draw/discard counts instead of repeating the same request. If a card cannot move, check its owner, scene and current revision.

title: Encounters, initiative and turns
summary: Set up a scene encounter and advance turns with the campaign system in mind.
text: Prepare an encounter Combat is associated with a scene. The host provides an encounter tracker; the selected RPG system can supply initiative configuration and rule-specific behavior. Do not assume every system has the same initiative formula, effects or resources. 1. As GM, open the intended scene and the combat tracker. 2. Add the participating tokens or actors. Scene tokens must belong to that scene. 3. Configure the supported initiative input/formula, or enter initiative values manually. 4. Roll initiative for the intended scope where a formula is available, then inspect the order. 5. Set hidden or defeated flags as needed and start the encounter. 6. Advance turns and rounds using the tracker. Stop the encounter when it is over. An encounter supports up to 64 combatants. Starting requires at least one; rolling initiative requires a configured formula. Share turn responsibility The GM manages order, combatants and encounter configuration. A player can advance the current turn only when the encounter is active and they control its current combatant. A visible combatant is not necessarily controlled by that account. Defeated combatants are skipped during normal advancement. If every combatant is defeated, there is no eligible next combatant. Adding or reordering entries should not be used as a substitute for selecting the intended current turn. Effects and previous turns Effects and conditions may advance at turn/round boundaries according to their system and configuration. Returning to a previous turn changes tracker history; it is not a general undo of all rule automation or resource changes already committed. Inspect affected sheets when correcting a mistaken advancement. Troubleshoot If initiative cannot roll, check the system's formula and required sheet values. If a player cannot end their turn, check token/actor control and the currently selected combatant. If combat appears absent after switching maps, reopen the encounter for the correct scene. Reconnect after a revision conflict and work from the current tracker rather than forcing old order data.

title: Compendiums and reusable content
summary: Collect reusable campaign material, lock finished packs and import compatible entries.
text: What a compendium contains A compendium is a reusable content pack rather than a full installation backup. Campaign packs can contain supported actors, items, journals, scenes and decks. Installed system packages may also provide catalogs. The core's generic item support does not mean the native PDF system includes item types. Build a campaign pack 1. As GM, create a compendium with a meaningful name. 2. Add the supported campaign resources you want to reuse. 3. Inspect entries and any linked media in a test import. 4. Choose whether the pack is shared with players. 5. Lock a finished pack to prevent accidental editing; unlock it before changing its entries. A portable entry can include its supported dependency graph and linked assets. This does not promise that every third-party module's private state can be transferred. Imported references are mapped into the destination campaign instead of granting access to the original campaign. Import an entry Open the appropriate pack and inspect the intended entry. As GM, import it into the current campaign. Check the new document, its images and its permissions before sharing it. A pack associated with another system cannot be imported as though its schema belonged to the current system. Import creates campaign content. Later editing of that copy is distinct from maintaining the source pack; do not assume it stays synchronized with a publisher's next release. Troubleshoot and respect content rights If a player cannot see a pack, inspect shared/access settings. If the GM cannot edit it, check its lock. If import reports a system mismatch, choose the matching campaign/system rather than renaming IDs. Missing media needs investigation of the source entry and import result, not a public alias for private storage. Only distribute content you own or are authorized to redistribute. A reusable structure, installed package or book purchase does not authorize including proprietary rules catalogs, books or licensed artwork in a public pack. Keep an installation backup as well: compendiums do not preserve all campaign history, accounts or host configuration.

title: Systems, modules and the marketplace
summary: Install trusted packages and understand the difference between host installation and table activation.
text: Choose the package type Type Responsibility Who selects it --- --- --- RPG system Sheets, document types and its own rules/content Owner installs; campaign selects the system Browser module Table tools and interface extensions Owner installs; GM activates for the table Trusted Django app Server-wide extension Owner activates with a managed restart The native PDF system remains available without a marketplace. Installing a system does not include every book or catalog for that game. Install a package 1. As installation owner, open Systems or Modules in the library. 2. Choose Install to browse the configured marketplace, or Install from ZIP for a local package you explicitly trust. 3. Inspect author, version, compatibility, permissions and license. Marketplace discovery shows the newest compatible, non-revoked release per package. 4. Wait for installation to finish, then refresh the installed library if the connection was interrupted. 5. Select the system for the campaign, or have its GM activate the browser module in Settings → Extensions . 6. Reload existing clients when required and test with both GM and player accounts. Installing a new version does not automatically replace the exact release active in every table. Activation is a separate selection. Server apps require the owner's server-wide activation and managed restart. Trust and language Browser module JavaScript executes on the application's origin. Signatures validate package provenance and integrity; they do not sandbox the code. A local ZIP installation is the owner's trust decision and still undergoes archive and compatibility validation. English is the default interface language. Available language packages/settings and system catalogs determine translations; user-authored names and notes are not translated automatically. Preserve each user's explicit language choice. Browse and search in your language 1. The owner installs and activates the compatible Translator language package for the installation. It is managed globally rather than enabled as a campaign extension. Reload existing pages after activation. 2. In account Settings , choose English, Portuguese (Brazil) or Spanish from the available languages. This is each account's own preference; another signed-in account does not inherit it. 3. Open Systems or Modules , then its installation browser. Marketplace category names and package tag badges follow the selected language. Categories belong to the selected package type and sort by their displayed labels. 4. Search by an original tag or its translated label in either the installed library or the marketplace. For example, Translation and Tradução can find the same tagged package. Clear the category or use All packages when checking the full catalog. Translation changes presentation only. Package IDs, original tags, signed records and category-filter identities stay intact. Package and publisher names, descriptions, acronyms and custom tags without a translation stay as authored. Long tags wrap on small screens. Without an active language package, the interface uses English; disabling it returns to English on the next page load. The installed library stays available when catalog discovery is offline. Troubleshoot An empty marketplace may mean missing catalog/key configuration or unavailable networking; installed packages remain separate from discovery. Do not disable verification to fix a rejected archive. Confirm the host version and package requirements. Before changing a system, back up and inspect existing actor data and compendiums; switching systems does not automatically convert all documents into another RPG's format.

title: Map Builder: from project to playable scene
summary: Build an editable map, manage assets and publish changes without losing the project.
text: Project, preview and scene Only a current campaign GM can edit Builder projects. Open Scenes → New scene → Map Builder . Entering the editor preserves the players' current broadcast. A project stores editable work; generation produces the native scene used in play. Action What it changes --- --- Autosave / Ctrl+S The editable project Preview A temporary view including all project layers Generate scene A new private native scene Update scene The same linked native scene Activate for players Scene visibility and the player broadcast Open an existing scene or Universal VTT map Use Edit Scene on the table to open the current scene's linked project or adopt its compatible native geometry. Adoption and Import Universal VTT share the native scene adapter. A Builder import creates a linked scene and editable project; a scene-directory import creates only the scene, which can be adopted later. A flattened background remains one image: source brushes and artwork layers cannot be reconstructed. Review import warnings and test the grid, doors and lights before player activation. See Universal VTT (wiki:universal-vtt). Build your first room 1. Name the project in the header. Set dimensions, cell size and background in Panels → Settings . 2. Choose Tiles for grid-oriented materials or Painting for softer terrain work. Configure the brush in Panels → Tools . 3. Import authorized images in Library → Import and classify them as floor, wall, door or object. Families and collections help organize reusable materials. 4. Paint the floor, draw walls and doors and add objects, lights or effects. A door is an independent segment; uploading a map image does not detect its walls. 5. Use Panels → Layers to select, name, lock or hide editor layers. Use Panels → Selection for selected-element properties. 6. Wait for the saved status, then inspect Preview . Hidden editor layers still appear in preview and generation. 7. Choose Generate scene . Later reopen the project through Panels → Projects or Edit with MapBuilder on its linked scene, then choose Update scene . 8. Activate the scene for players when ready. Import a finished image Choose Library → Import → Import ready-made map , select an upload or existing campaign image and enter map dimensions in cells and cell size. This creates a background beneath your additions. It does not reconstruct the image's original objects. Changing the background preserves existing coordinates; a dimension change that would exclude objects is refused. Edit an object's properties, appearance and behavior Select the element and right-click it, press Shift+F10 or use the keyboard's context-menu key. On touch screens, open Panels → Selection → Object options . The same menu offers Properties , Appearance and Behavior , plus the native editor, Edit nodes , torch components or presence filters when that element supports them. Duplicate , Rotate and Delete are also available. Use Properties for the element's name and supported settings, Appearance for its artwork and visual configuration, and Behavior for its interaction. Enter or leave a name field to apply it; Escape discards that field's pending edit. Names of up to 120 characters keep the element's identity and node connections. Applied property changes save automatically and can be undone. Objects and Empty Objects also offer Ready-made models ; follow Smart Objects (wiki:smart-objects) for all 14 models and their editable nodes. Valid graph edits save automatically too. Close or Escape waits for pending valid changes; an invalid field stays open for correction. Saving configuration does not operate the mechanism. Use Generate scene or Update scene explicitly to publish project changes. Arrange a group and save reusable objects Select objects with Shift-click or a selection rectangle, then open Builder tools in the header. 1. Enter a Group name and choose Group selection in a layer . Use Project layers to move, hide, lock or select that group. 2. Under Align and distribute , align edges or centers. Select at least three objects for equal-gap distribution. Enter an angle and choose Rotate selection to rotate the group together. Locked layers, invalid bounds or overlapping doors leave the selection unchanged. 3. Under My objects , enter a Preset name and choose Save selection to My objects . The model includes its artwork, linked components, activation areas and Smart Object graphs. 4. In this or another project of the same campaign, choose Place for the saved model, then click the map. Escape cancels placement. Copies receive new identities and remap internal connections; keep the selection's references self-contained or bound to campaign resources. Deleting a saved model preserves copies already placed on maps. The library holds up to 128 models, with up to 100 selected objects per model. It belongs to this campaign. Paint objects and inspect activation areas Choose Objects in the library and select an uploaded object image or family. In Builder tools → Object brush , enable Paint multiple objects , then set spacing in cells and the size/rotation variation. Drag on the map to place repeated objects. Each completed stroke is one Undo step, and normal project limits still apply. Enable Show all object activation areas to compare named circular object guides and region rectangles without selecting each one. The overview respects layer visibility and isolation and is omitted from Preview and generated scenes. Configure the actual radius and enter/exit behavior in Smart Objects (wiki:smart-objects). Walk through the draft as a player Choose Builder tools → Test as player . Select a campaign Test actor when the behavior depends on a character, adjust Vision radius (cells) , then click or use arrow keys to move the test pawn. Check wall collisions and visibility, and choose Interact near an object. Crossing its activation area rehearses enter/exit events. The detached map applies the test results to a separate copy. Reset test discards those results; closing preserves the authored draft and the live scene. The server rolls back behavior changes and sends no sounds, messages or camera effects to players. Timers do not advance, and this generic rehearsal does not simulate RPG rules or replace checking a real player's permissions. Generate/update the scene and test an actual player account before activating it for the group. Useful controls V selects; F returns to floor painting; E removes an entire object. Area floor erasing is a separate tool. Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Shift+Z/Ctrl+Y redoes, Space + drag pans, the wheel zooms and 0 fits the map. / adjusts the brush. With the floor brush active, Shift + left drag changes its size without painting; Escape cancels that adjustment. Bring tabletop edits back into the project 1. Edit a generated element in the game, then reopen its project, return to the Builder tab or request Update scene . Compatible manual changes to names, geometry, artwork, lights, effects and Blueprints are imported at those points. 2. Inspect the imported result. Deleted generated objects disappear from the project; split wall spans remain independently editable. Manually added scene objects stay separate from the editable source. 3. Continue editing and wait for the saved status. Changes to different properties merge with pending local work. Undoing your local edit preserves imported game changes. 4. If both sides changed the same property differently, synchronization stops with your local draft preserved. Choose Reload saved project to adopt the server version or Save a copy to retain your work as a new project. Unsupported object-type changes or geometry also stop with a diagnostic; do not force an older revision over the scene. 5. Review and choose Update scene . It requires current project and scene revisions and remains a GM operation. Synchronizing or saving does not execute behaviors or change the player broadcast. Updating preserves scene-only tokens, images, lights, effects, drawings and fog, plus the scene's name, folder, visibility, broadcast and environment. Keep map dimensions and cell size unchanged when manual scene content exists. Live door state is preserved; lights, effects and other runtime settings retain their live values when their authored defaults are unchanged. Deliberately changing an authored default applies it on update. Automated Move/Rotate actions leave source geometry unchanged, so an update reapplies authored positions and angles. Save, recover and respect limits Autosave records completed edits after a short pause; the header shows waiting, saving or saved. Ctrl+S synchronizes immediately. Returning to the game waits for pending saves; a failure keeps the editor open for retry or explicit discard. A lost response retries the same operation rather than creating another write. A revision conflict pauses saving and keeps the draft: use the explicit reload/copy choices above. Discard changes removes only unacknowledged work. If the initial project or library load fails, use Retry ; editing stays blocked so an empty replacement is not created. Projects allow 32 layers, 2,000 combined objects, 256 classified images and a 1 MB document. Dimensions are 1–200 cells and 16–256 pixels per cell, subject to a shared 16,777,216-pixel image limit or a smaller host limit. Image uploads are limited to 25 MB and 40 million decoded pixels. Maximum dimensions cannot all be used simultaneously. A browser draft is recovery help, not a backup. Remove asset deletes the campaign resource and may affect other maps; Undo cannot restore the deleted file. Players and streamers cannot edit Builder projects; test player interaction separately from GM editing.

title: Smart Objects: models, nodes and safe playtests
summary: Start with an interactive model, customize its logic and test behavior before applying it to the game.
text: Start with an event Doors, objects, levers, torches, Empty Objects and presence regions share a visual blueprint editor. Select a starting event, connect its output to a node and configure explicit actions. An empty authored interaction graph does nothing: no implicit toggle is added. Doors offer On interact and On destroy . Objects also support On area enter/exit ; regions offer area entry/exit and destruction. Named signals provide On signal . An event starts execution; it does not compare a state or choose an image by itself. Legacy state-specific interaction/entry/exit graphs and change events are discarded rather than migrated; recreate their behavior with current events and logic nodes. Turn uploaded artwork into a Smart Object Import your image through the library, classify it as an Object and place it on the map. With Selection or Objects active, double-click it with the left mouse button to open its Blueprint. You can also choose Edit nodes in its context menu or Smart object in its Behavior properties. Existing artwork, geometry and any authored behavior are preserved. Build your own graph there, or use the ready-made catalog when it suits the mechanism. Activate effects when a token crosses an area 1. Select the object and open Panels → Selection . 2. Enable Circular activation area and set Activation radius (cells) . The circle is centered on the object and moves with it; its radius is independent of the image dimensions. 3. Open the Blueprint and connect On area enter or On area exit to the intended light, sound, message or other supported action. Area events need no direct click on the artwork. 4. Test a token entering, leaving and crossing the whole area. A path across the entire circle can produce both events. Use conditions if the effect should run only for the first arrival, last departure or a matching token. The area guide is for the GM in the editor. Builder tools → Show all object activation areas compares several guides without selecting each object. An area defines where events may trigger; its graph defines what those events do. An empty graph performs no effect. Choose one of the 14 ready-made models Select an Object or Empty Object and open Object options → Ready-made models , choose a model in Behavior , or open Object catalog in the node editor. These entry points share the same editable catalog. Model Starting behavior --- --- Interactive switch Toggle the object and optionally a linked door Chest Open/close and show a message on its first opening Secret passage Toggle a required linked door Readable book Open an authorized journal handout for chosen recipients Altar Show a message with a five-second cooldown Warning trap Warn on token entry while armed; interact to arm/disarm Bell Notify chosen recipients with a short cooldown Pressure plate Open a linked door on entry; close when the last token leaves Dice challenge Ask selected recipients to roll explicitly Quest giver Set a bound quest active and open its journal entry Quest completion Set a bound quest completed and open its journal entry Entrance sign Show a message on first entry; interact to read it again Timed switch Activate, optionally open a door, then reset after a delay Door button Open a linked door when pressed Search the catalog, choose the model and supply its required door, journal/quest, recipients, message, expression or delay. Add a sound when activated enables a campaign sound and volume; Use an active image enables another Object image for the active state. Leaving either unchecked adds no corresponding override. The inactive state keeps the original image, and Empty Objects remain image-free. Choose Apply , inspect the generated nodes and customize them as needed. Applying preserves the object's identity and geometry as one Undo step; closing the catalog without applying leaves it unchanged. Replacing existing authored nodes requires confirmation. The warning trap reports a warning: damage, RPG checks, item consumption and system-specific rewards belong to the RPG system package, not these generic models. Build a door toggle 1. Select On interact and connect Check state , configured to compare Closed . 2. Connect True → Change state: Opened . 3. Connect False → Change state: Closed . 4. Add Control light , Play sound or Change image after the appropriate action when desired. 5. Bind another target using a typed Element reference , Light reference or compatible group. Without a target connection, element actions normally address the edited element. 6. Simulate both initial states, then run a server playtest before updating the scene. Value nodes supply typed data; they do not execute a chain by themselves. Compare state/value , All conditions and Any condition can feed the Boolean Test input of a decision. Sequence runs its branches in order; Choose path selects a typed case; Random selects a weighted branch. Change a native shader from a behavior First add the shader to the map, either independently or as a torch component. Open the controlling object's Blueprint and choose Add node → Control shader . Select the shader from this map, choose a property and enter the intended value. Connect the interaction, area event, signal or preceding action to the node's execution input. Chain separate nodes when changing multiple properties. Supported properties are enabled state, color, intensity, opacity, speed, scale, radius, rotation, light response and light emission. For example, connect On area enter → Control shader , choose Opacity and set 0.35 . Use a separate exit action if leaving should restore the prior appearance. A connected Value input must match the property: Boolean for enabled state, Text for a six-digit hex color, Number for numeric properties. A typed variable can supply that value; the server applies the native property's limits. Torch visibility and flame state still gate the component shader. Changing its parameters while the torch is off does not ignite it; its enabled setting is retained for when the flame is visible. Rehearsal reports the shader changes without saving them. Updating a scene preserves live values for Builder parameters you left unchanged; an explicit edit to a Builder parameter applies that authored value. See the node reference (docs:map-builder) for bounds and target behavior. Remember a puzzle with variables and signals Use Get variable/Set variable with a case-sensitive name, scope This element or Scene , and type Boolean, Number or Text. For example, set scene Boolean PuzzleSolved to True, then emit the named signal PuzzleSolved . A receiving On signal graph reads that variable and opens its passage. Each event reads an initial state/variable snapshot. A later read inside that same event still sees the initial value; the next queued receiving event sees the assignment. A signal alone does not open a door, carries no custom payload and remains inside the scene. Configure the receiver's action explicitly. GM Automation → Variables inspects memory; resetting a variable removes that entry without running a graph. Area events run for eligible token crossings. A token crossing the entire area can cause entry and exit in one accepted move. Use event context and conditions when you want only the first arrival or last departure to matter. Interact with object explicitly runs a target's interaction behavior; Change state alone does not run another graph or its image/sound actions. Request a roll or advance a quest For Request dice roll , choose the native expression, optional label, recipients and result visibility. The server checks membership and scene access before delivering each request. The recipient must press Roll ; streamers cannot receive an actionable prompt. Retrying or opening another tab reuses the recipient's logical roll. The graph continues without waiting for a result. See Chat and dice (wiki:chat-dice) for native notation. For Open journal , bind a campaign journal, quest or board and choose recipients who already have access. Opening it does not grant permission to read it. Set quest status binds one fixed campaign quest and desired status authored by the GM. A player can trigger that configured change through the object without gaining general journal editing rights. Check the quest's own visibility and permissions separately; see Journals and quests (wiki:journals). Connect clocks, clues and mind maps The Control clock and Control clue nodes bind a fixed campaign resource and action, respecting campaign/current-scene scope. A GM authors the effect; a player interaction delegates only that configured progress action, without general configuration rights. Unfinished clues and GM notes stay protected. Open mind map opens a selected map, optionally focused on a topic, for the triggering user, players or selected recipients. Each recipient must already have access. Control mind-map topic completes, resets or toggles a bound topic through the native service. All four bindings require an active campaign GM; server rehearsal rolls back effects, receipts and notifications. Simulation describes the action, and delayed work checks targets again when it runs. See clocks (wiki:clocks), clues (wiki:clues) and mind maps (wiki:mindmaps). Use time deliberately Delay persists a continuation; Timer is a named one-shot countdown whose expiry runs the matching named signal. They survive closed browsers/server restarts, and pausing scene automation keeps pending jobs waiting. GM Automation → Waiting shows the queue. Behavior changes, removed targets or lost access can cancel pending work. Exports, campaign snapshots and copies omit these jobs; a full database backup includes them. Simulate, playtest and publish Simulate is a local graph preview. Test behavior runs the server engine against the unsaved Builder document or a live element, showing predicted state, variable and cross-element changes. Choose an optional test actor/token for token-dependent actions. Tests use GM permissions, so also test a real player separately. Tests roll everything back and deliver no live sounds, messages, handouts, roll prompts or camera changes. Quest changes and roll requests appear in the report without saving quest state or opening recipient windows. Delay stops at the wait; Timer scheduling is listed without advancing time or firing receivers. Verify actual timing in a controlled live scene. After successful editing, wait for autosave and choose Generate scene/Update scene ; returning to the table alone does not apply project graphs. Limits and troubleshooting Each event graph allows 32 nodes and 64 connections; a door's graphs allow 128 nodes combined. A scope stores up to 64 variables. Delay/Timer share 64 pending jobs per scene and 256 per campaign. Cycles, invalid typed connections and oversized chains are rejected. If nothing happens, check the starting event, connected actions, targets, pause state and Automation log . A player-triggered chain cannot lock/unlock by default; the GM must explicitly allow player locking/unlocking on that state action. A missing target can be skipped with a diagnostic. Teleport is within the same scene; these tools do not promise cross-scene or group transport.

title: Import and export Universal VTT
summary: Bring in a prepared map or transfer a native scene while understanding the format limits.
text: Choose the right interchange Universal VTT imports .uvtt , .dd2vtt and .df2vtt files with supported image, grid, walls, doors and lights. Only a campaign GM may import/export. Imported scenes start GM-only and preserve the existing player broadcast. Choose Import Universal VTT inside Builder to create a linked native scene and editable project. The editor saves the current draft first and opens the imported project separately. Choose Scenes → New scene → Import Universal VTT when you only need a native scene; later use Edit with MapBuilder to adopt it. Compatible geometry and lights remain editable, while the flattened artwork stays one background image. For a PNG/JPEG/WebP/TIFF image you want to decorate in the Builder, use Import ready-made map instead. An image cannot reconstruct original walls or layers. Import a scene 1.
