The GM sees its faint marker on every tab, and selects or edits it on the GM tab. It remains editable in the builder, and is omitted from player/streamer scene data. Older scenes receive the same private presentation immediately, without requiring regeneration. Native edits, copies and scene updates keep it on GM. Players still trigger its authored area events by moving their tokens; delayed area/signal actions keep their original player permissions. Direct player clicks cannot activate it. It cannot receive its own image. The node catalog is the same for every element kind: Change sprite and Set appearance can control another object through an explicit Target connection. Visual nodes without a compatible target remain editable drafts and are skipped with a diagnostic when executed. Undo/Redo, automatic saving and scene updates keep its identity and behavior. For ordinary images, levers and torches, use Move to GM image layer in the context menu to hide them. Switch to GM , right-click the object and choose Move to image layer to return it to the game. The Images tab edits public images; private images are selected on GM. Returning a mixed selection leaves Empty Objects on GM. Private images and Empty Object markers remain visible to the GM at 55% opacity across tabs; private drawings also multiply their authored opacity by 55%. Players and streamers receive none of these private elements. Changing tabs updates editing controls without rebuilding the rendered scene. Automatic saving Project edits save automatically after a short pause: map name, completed brush strokes, object and layer edits, settings, Undo and Redo. The header shows whether changes are waiting, saving or saved. Background writes preserve the current selection and history and do not interrupt drawing. The status button and Ctrl+S remain available to synchronize immediately. Smart Object graphs also apply valid edits automatically. There is no manual Save/Cancel step: Close or Escape waits for pending valid edits. Invalid fields remain visible for correction and block closing. Undo/Redo changes are also saved. Opening or closing an unchanged current graph does not create an empty blueprint. Removed event graphs are discarded when older data is loaded. A lost response retries the same logical operation and UUID, so a confirmed write is not repeated. A revision conflict pauses automatic saving and preserves the local draft. Reload saved project explicitly adopts the current server version; Save a copy preserves the local map under a new identity. Failed saving keeps edits in the current tab and offers recovery controls. In a live Smart Object conflict, further writes pause until the editor is reopened with the current version; its stale revision guard is never replaced silently. Discard changes discards only changes that have not been acknowledged. Reloading this tab recovers an uncertain write by confirming its original receipt before sending newer local edits. Older drafts without that write's body pause for explicit reload or copy. If the initial library or project load fails, editing stays blocked and Retry reloads it without creating an empty replacement project. Correcting or undoing a rejected edit clears that rejected save attempt, so reloading does not report it as an uncertain write. After reconnecting, Retry in a Smart Object editor also resumes the pending project save with its original receipt; revision conflicts still require explicit recovery. Returning to the game waits for pending project changes. If saving fails, the editor stays open so the GM can retry or explicitly discard. Automatic saving persists configuration; it does not generate a scene or execute graph actions. Generate scene and Update scene remain explicit actions. Editing a live element applies its graph configuration to that owner and linked source through their existing revision checks, without operating the mechanism. Update a generated scene Keep the project to edit the map later. Generate scene creates its first scene; afterward the primary header action becomes Update scene . Reopening the project from the game's scene directory updates that same scene rather than creating another one. The header action and Panels → Review → Update scene replace the tiled background and the resources generated by this project in its linked scene. Manually placed tokens, images, lights, particles, shaders, drawings, fog and other scene content remain in place. Scene name, folder, visibility, broadcast and environment settings remain VTT choices. Existing native doors keep their live open/closed/locked state during an update. Lights, particles and shaders also retain their live enabled state when the corresponding authored enabled setting has not changed. An intentional change to that setting in the project applies on update. Secret-door discovery follows the same rule: runtime discovery is preserved while the authored discovered setting stays unchanged; an intentional project change is applied on update. Authorized Move/Rotate actions acknowledge their native geometry in ownership history while leaving the editable source unchanged; updating the scene reapplies authored positions and angles. Manual VTT edits to generated objects are imported when the project opens, when returning to its browser tab and before updating the scene. Compatible changes to names, geometry, artwork, lights, effects and Blueprints appear in the editable project; deleted generated objects disappear from it. Split wall spans remain independently editable. Manual objects added directly to the scene remain separate from the project. Runtime interaction settings are preserved when their authored default is unchanged, and an intentional authored change applies on update. Region enabled state stays live while authored enabled/layer settings remain unchanged; an intentional authored change wins. Configuration updates quietly baseline occupancy rather than firing presence graphs. Updates and synchronization require both current project and scene revisions. Changes to different properties merge with pending project edits. Undo keeps imported game changes while undoing local edits. If the same property was edited differently in both places, synchronization stops and keeps the local draft; use Reload saved project or Save a copy to resolve it. Object type changes and geometry the project cannot represent also stop with a specific diagnostic. Changes that race with rendering still require a fresh synchronization. Keep map dimensions and cell size unchanged when the scene contains manually placed content. Existing version 1/2 projects can acquire ownership history if their original generated IDs, native data and grid geometry still match exactly, allowing only live door-state changes. Opening the project checks eligibility without writing; saving records the proven ownership before replacing its old source. Without that proof, the legacy linked scene cannot be updated from this project. The builder never infers ownership from nearby or visually similar objects. Use a new project when authoring an independent scene. Uploaded image assets remain in the campaign library. Goal Reference --- --- Make a switch or linked torch Levers ( levers), Composed torches ( composed-torches) Trigger actions when tokens enter/leave Regions and pressure plates ( regions-and-pressure-plates), Empty Objects ( empty-objects) Share conditions or coordinate objects Composite conditions ( composite-conditions), Variables and named signals ( variables-and-named-signals) Wait, count or restrict repetition Persistent execution controls ( persistent-execution-controls), Delay ( persistent-delay), Timer ( persistent-timer) Reuse or inspect behavior Templates ( reusable-behavior-templates), Scene network ( scene-network), Server rehearsal ( test-behavior-through-the-server) Change a surface, present a message or move the triggering token Dynamic surfaces ( dynamic-surfaces), Messages/handouts ( messages-handouts-and-camera-focus), Teleport ( same-scene-teleport) The following reference covers the shared node editor and its supported element adapters. The design direction (smart-objects-direction.md) records proposals; it is not a list of additional controls available in this checkout. Door Smart Objects Each element owns its blueprint. Doors, levers, torches and presence regions share the editor, reusable behavior templates and the GM's scene network view. The editor uses the application's existing modal system and shows the actual element instance. Double-click an editable door on the Map Builder canvas to open Smart object . The modal has three areas: the Events list on the left, the graph canvas in the middle, and appearance settings and Simulation on the right. These areas stack on narrow screens. The instance node shows the element's name and actual current state. Doors offer On interaction ( onInteract ) and On destroy ( onDestroy ). Objects, including levers, torches and Empty Objects, also offer On area enter ( onAreaEnter ) and On area exit ( onAreaExited ). Regions offer On area enter ( onAreaEnter ), On area exit ( onAreaExited ) and On destroy . Named signals provide On signal ( onSignal ). Geometry and the initial state remain editable in Selection . Events only start their connected sequence. They do not compare values, choose a state or change the image. Use logic nodes for decisions and action nodes for changes. A mechanism with a blueprint and an empty interaction graph does nothing when activated; it has no automatic toggle. For a complete lever toggle, connect On interaction → Check state: Deactivated . Connect True → Change state: Activated → Change sprite with the active image, and False → Change state: Deactivated → Change sprite with the inactive image. Both state and image actions belong to this same sequence. For a torch, use Normal/Turned ; its flame remains an independent action. Conditions read the state at the start of the event, even after a state action. Default appearance by state remains a separate optional visual setting. Area events start for every eligible token crossing the boundary. The region's occupancy changes only on first arrival and last departure; first/last tests belong in logic nodes. A region has no direct interaction port. Editing configuration does not start gameplay sequences. For an object, its authored size and rotation define the area. A token's center entering or leaving that box starts the corresponding graph, including both events when an accepted movement passes completely through the area. Area events do not toggle the object or change its image. Use Event context for the triggering token and presence count, and explicit condition/action nodes for the response. Moving, resizing, rotating or importing objects quietly refreshes membership. Simulate and Test behavior also support both object area events. To reuse another object's configured behavior, connect the area's event to Interact with object , then connect an Element reference to its Target . This explicitly runs that target's On interaction graph, including connected state, sprite, light and sound actions. Change state changes only the state; it does not call another event or replay the target's sprite actions. Native objects without a blueprint keep their normal toggle, while an authored empty interaction graph does nothing. Interaction chains share the existing limits, transaction and retry receipt. Test behavior rehearses the complete chain; local Simulate lists the requested interaction without running other graphs. The target interaction is queued after the source event's actions, like named signals. It follows the target's existing logic, including any authored toggle. Autosave stores edits in the project. When the project is linked to a scene, click Update scene to apply changed graphs to the game. Returning to the game alone does not update that scene. The save status and behavior editor state this distinction; updates keep the same scene ID. On signal ( onSignal ) receives a named signal from Emit event or a one-shot timer with the same name. Select a named signal to expose its port on the instance node. The authored signal name remains unchanged. There is no separate timer-expiry event ID: existing signal:<name graphs remain the receivers. On destroy runs immediately before an explicit in-game deletion, including selection deletion or clearing a native layer. It can switch another light, change another element or notify a named signal receiver while the owner still exists. Removal and its effects share one transaction; a failed graph keeps the owner and rolls back its effects. Retrying the same command reuses its receipt. One command can remove at most 32 owners with connected destruction handlers. Only authorized native editing commands remove elements. Paused automation removes the element without executing its destruction graph. Removing an element in the Builder, updating a generated scene, changing configuration or deleting an asset or campaign does not execute this gameplay event. Timers and waits owned by a removed element are cancelled. For effects that must continue later, send a signal to another surviving element and schedule the work there. Test behavior predicts the removal and shows Removed for this test , while keeping the real map, project and history intact. Each state has three appearance options: - Native appearance: use the door's material while closed or locked and hide its image while open. - Hidden image: hide the image in that state, retaining the native geometry. - Use image: choose a project image classified as Door for that state, including an image to display while open. Events offers only the supported starting events and their node counts. There are no event-level state filters. Loading earlier data discards onChange and state-specific entry, exit and interaction graphs; it does not migrate their actions. Elements and asset files remain in place. Rebuild those sequences under On interaction , an area event or a named signal. Appearance selection remains independent of the chosen graph. Each event occupies one row on the instance node, with its socket on the right. Its cable leaves horizontally from that socket. Drag from an event port to start that event's branch, even when another event is selected. A line follows the pointer. Release it on empty canvas to open the node chooser at that position; choosing a type creates the node and connects it to the branch. Add node , or a double-click on empty canvas, opens the same chooser without a connection. Type in its search field to filter the list: text found in a node's name or description ranks first, and letters typed in order within the node name also match, so pls finds Play sound . Enter picks the best match and the arrow keys move between options. State and visual actions apply directly in the current sequence; a state change does not start another graph. Interact with object and Emit event queue the target's graph. Their Next output continues the source sequence before that queued graph runs, within the same command. A chain is limited to 32 element operations and 4 on the same element. Receivers of a Scene-scope signal use a separate budget of 256 deliveries, so one broadcast can reach many listeners; each receiver still counts toward its 4 operations. Exceeding any bound fails the whole command without persisting anything, and the automation log shows the chain with the bound that was reached: an element that ran more than 4 times (a repeating chain), more than 32 element operations (a long chain) or more than 256 scene-signal deliveries. A chain started by a player never locks or unlocks a door unless the GM sets that Change state action's Locks option to Players may lock or unlock : then a lever operated by a player can unlock another door, and an interaction graph on a locked door can open it. Without the option the operation is skipped and logged. Barrier changes are play state, like the door state: scene updates keep them. A reference whose door was deleted stays in the graph marked Missing door ; the action that needs it is skipped and logged as Missing target . Pick on map , on an Element reference or Set light node, steps the modal aside: click the door or light on the builder map to choose it, or press Escape or Cancel to keep the current target. Duplicating doors together points copied references at the copies; references to doors outside the copied group keep their target. Value nodes have no Input or Next; they are evaluated when an executed node reads them. Their diamond sockets carry a type, State (violet) or True or False (cyan), with one source per input. For example, connect Get property: Current state → Compare state: Locked → Check state · Test , and start Check state from On interaction . Its True branch can change the state and play an unlock sound. Current state for simulation supplies the initial snapshot for a local test; it is not a filter or parameter on the event. Change sprite is an image action in the sequence. Change state → Change sprite in onInteract applies the requested state and keeps the chosen image. To change another object's image from an area, connect On area enter → Change sprite , select Use image , and connect Element reference → Target to the object that should change. The target does not need an interaction graph. Connect On area exit → Change sprite: Native appearance to the same reference to restore it. An Element group can change several images together. This changes artwork only; it does not change state or run the target's events. Ordinary images retain their base image, layer and box privately while overridden; restoring their native appearance removes the override. Native move/resize keeps that restoration box in sync. Unchanged authored geometry preserves the override on Update scene ; native manual geometry changes retain the existing conflict guard. Empty Objects and regions remain image-free while controlling other elements. Nodes that need resources become available when those resources exist. The event itself does not compare, toggle or restore an image. Players receive only the resulting appearance. Lights and sounds must already exist in the project or campaign to be available as targets; otherwise the chooser keeps the type disabled and explains why. Other node types use the same catalog for every element kind. Sockets are the circles on node edges: the Input on the left and outputs on the right, colored by output ( Next gold, True green, False red; door ports identify their starting event). Connections take the color of their source. Drag from an output to an existing node's Input to connect them directly. Value connections can also start at the input: drag Target to an existing reference's Element output, or release on empty canvas to create a compatible reference. Clicking Target opens the same filtered chooser. Select Element reference , then choose the other object in its Element field or with Pick on map . This creates the target connection; connect the event separately to the action's Input . Enter or Space on a value input opens the chooser; Shift+Enter lets you select an existing compatible output with the keyboard. An already connected input keeps its connection until you remove it. Each output can start another branch. Press Escape , click outside the chooser or release outside the canvas to cancel the pending branch; creating no node leaves the graph unchanged. Clicking an output and then an Input remains available. With an output focused, Enter or Space opens the same node chooser. To connect to an existing input using the keyboard, press Shift+Enter on the output, use Tab to reach the Input , then press Enter . Actions continue through Next ; a condition has separate True and False outputs. Version 2 accepts multiple branches per output, evaluated depth-first in stored order; a shared node executes once per event. Conditions read the event's initial state, and action nodes execute in the stored sequence. Click a connection to remove it, or focus it and press Delete . Deleting a node with its × button, or with Delete on its focused header, removes its connections. Drag node headers to arrange the graph, or focus a header and use the arrow keys; Shift increases the keyboard movement. Saved positions start at the graph's top-left origin: moving a node past that edge keeps it on the edge and shifts the other nodes instead. Drag empty canvas or use the middle mouse button to pan; the wheel or a pinch zooms around the pointer. With the canvas focused, the arrow keys pan, + and − zoom and 0 frames the graph. The controls at the bottom right show the zoom level, which resets to 100% when clicked, and Fit graph frames all nodes. Undo and Redo in the modal toolbar ( Ctrl+Z , Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y ) step through edits, including connections, nodes, parameters, positions and appearances; valid results save automatically. Click a card to select it; Shift, Ctrl or Cmd adds or removes cards, and Shift+drag on empty canvas draws a selection rectangle. Ctrl+A selects every card. Dragging any selected header, or the arrow keys on its focused header, moves the whole selection, and Delete removes the selected nodes and their connections; the event node stays. Ctrl+C copies the selected nodes with the connections between them, Ctrl+V pastes them at the pointer, also into another event or door while the page stays open, and Ctrl+D duplicates them beside the originals. Moving cards past the graph's top or left edge keeps them on the edge and shifts the other nodes in every event. The minimap at the bottom left shows all cards and the visible area; click or drag it to move the view. For example, connect On interaction → Check state: Closed → True → Change state: Opened → Change sprite → Play sound → Set light . Choose the open-door image, a sound and the room's light, leaving the light enabled. The interaction starts the sequence, the condition chooses a branch and the actions change the door, sound and light. Simulate highlights the executed nodes and connections and lists their actions under Simulation locally. It does not operate the scene, play audio or change lights. Valid blueprint edits apply and save automatically. Close waits for pending edits; it does not undo acknowledged changes. Use Undo/Redo to revise them. Invalid fields must be corrected before closing. The generated door uses its existing native door_state for collision, vision, lighting and sound propagation. The server validates targets and graph limits, then executes effects inside the existing transaction and command receipt. A retry cannot repeat the effects. Reading, reconnecting or reopening a scene restores its current appearance without replaying actions. A state request does not start a new event; interaction is a separate starting event. Players retain their existing door permissions: a configured interaction on a locked door may play its effects, but cannot unlock the door or change it to another state. Light actions require dynamic lighting to be enabled. The GM receives the graphs; players and streamers receive only the current presentation. Image delivery follows that state's visible appearance, including the existing rules for undiscovered secret or invisible doors. Duplicating a door preserves its blueprint. Duplicating a group with a targeted light remaps the new door to the copied light; a door copied alone keeps the existing target. Composite conditions Add node → Logic includes All conditions ( all , AND) and Any condition ( any , OR). Their four Boolean inputs A–D accept Compare state results or another composite node. Connect two to four inputs; unconnected inputs are ignored. A draft with zero or one connected input remains editable and evaluates False. The node shows its connection count and explains the minimum. Connect Result to Check state → Test , and connect the event's execution wire to that Check state's Input . Composite nodes have no execution sockets. For a three-torch passage, read each torch's Current state , compare it with Turned , and connect those three results to All's A , B and C . Use Element reference → Get property · Target for the other torches; an unconnected Get property Target reads the edited torch itself. Route the Check state's True branch to a Change state action targeting the passage door. To close it again when a torch returns, route False to Closed and evaluate the same rule in each torch's On interaction sequence. Each torch needs the rule so an interaction checks the combination. Conditions read the initial event snapshot; choose the branch explicitly when its actions also turn that torch. All/Any evaluate current conditions, without counting activations or waiting for several events. Repeatedly turning one torch cannot replace another torch. Every connected input is evaluated in A–D order, and shared value nodes are read once per event. Simulate shows each result; the GM's Automation log records it during play. Generation, duplication, linked updates and campaign archives keep the typed connections and remap referenced elements. These are version-2 nodes; older blueprints are unchanged until an explicit meaningful edit. Variables and named signals Get variable and Set variable use a case-sensitive name, Scope ( This element or Scene ) and Value type ( True or False , Number or Text ). Element memory belongs to the edited door, lever, torch or region; scene memory is shared by the scene's elements. Get variable returns its Default value when nothing has been stored. Reading a default does not create stored memory. Set variable uses its configured value or a connected Value of the same type. False, zero and empty text are valid values. A name keeps the same type within its scope; reset existing memory before changing its type. Connect Get variable to Compare value , then its Boolean Result to Check state → Test . Boolean and text comparisons offer Equals and Not equals; numbers also offer Less than, Less than or equal, Greater than and Greater than or equal. An unconnected Compare value reads False, 0 or empty text for its selected type. Changing a node's type removes incompatible value wires as one undo step, so reconnect them with the new type. Each event reads an initial snapshot of memory. Assignments are applied after that graph is evaluated: a Get variable in the same event still reads its initial value, while the next event sees the assignment. For a persistent puzzle, an interaction can set a scene Boolean PuzzleSolved to True, then emit PuzzleSolved ; a receiving graph can read that variable and open a passage. The complete command, including assignments and receiving actions, commits atomically. Repeating its request does not repeat effects. In the event list, On signal → Signal name → Add signal creates a named receiving graph. Emit event with This element scope runs it on this element or the element connected to Target. Scene scope sends it to elements in the same scene that have that named graph. Receivers run from the bounded event queue after the sending event finishes; signals do not cross scenes or campaigns. A signal alone does not change an element's state. It carries its name, without custom payloads. Configure any desired state change in the receiving graph. Names use 1–64 ASCII characters, beginning with a letter, followed by letters, digits, underscores, dots or hyphens. Each scope stores at most 64 variables; numbers must be finite and between −1,000,000 and 1,000,000, and text is limited to 256 characters. Each blueprint has at most 16 named receiving graphs. These nodes and graphs require version 2; existing blueprints keep their compatibility. Simulation variables supplies private preview values. Simulation uses defaults when omitted and lists queued assignments and emissions; it neither writes game memory nor executes receiving graphs. Select a named graph to simulate that receiver separately. The GM's Automation → Variables view shows stored scene and element memory. Reset variable removes only that entry, without running events; the next read uses its authored default. A reset checks the displayed value and refuses if it changed, requiring a refresh before trying again. Players and streamers receive neither variable memory nor private graph details. Reopening a scene, linked builder updates and campaign archives preserve live memory. Duplicating a native element starts its own memory empty; scene memory remains shared. Editing a blueprint or resetting memory never emits a gameplay event. Groups and typed resource references Add node → Values → Element group stores a name of 1–80 characters and an ordered list of 1–32 unique members. Choose Elements , Lights or Sounds as its member type. Reorder or replace members without changing their identities; remove a member while keeping at least one. The typed Targets output applies compatible actions to each listed member in order. These are explicit saved lists, not live searches or a rule that all members must have fired an event. Element references and groups can include doors, levers, torches, ordinary live images and presence regions. Baked floor and wall pixels are outside this list. Images without a Smart Object state return no state from Get property . Get property accepts a single Element; it does not combine group states. State, flame, reveal, barrier, interaction, region and element-scoped signal actions accept an Element or element group, applying only supported capabilities. The GM log and Test behavior distinguish missing targets from existing targets that cannot perform an action, identifying the latter by name. A mixed group still applies the action to compatible members; incompatible and missing members are skipped. Execution traces keep these identities separately as targetIds , unsupportedIds and missingIds . Light reference connects a native light to Set light , Move object or Rotate object. Sound reference connects a campaign sound to Play sound or Control sound . Light and sound groups use the corresponding typed Target ports; they cannot be connected to an unrelated resource type. The configured light/sound in an action remains its fallback only when Target is disconnected. A connected missing reference is skipped without using that fallback or Self. Deleted members keep their UUID and appear as missing for repair; deleting a member does not silently redirect actions. Copies remap targets copied together and preserve external targets. Campaign sounds remain shared resources. Save, generation, linked updates and archives preserve group order and authored values. If an import omits audio, actors or tokens, their corresponding typed sound references/group members and presence-filter IDs receive fresh inert UUIDs. The same replacement is reused across project source, native objects and ownership history, keeping those targets unavailable for repair. Names and authored scalar text, including UUID-like text, stay unchanged. Move, rotate and interaction during play Move object uses relative X/Y cell offsets, each from −1,000 to 1,000. Rotate object adds an angle from −36,000 to 36,000 degrees around each target's own center; a door with a Rotation anchor point pivots on that anchor. Without Target, these act on the owning element; connected targets may be an Element, Light or their typed groups. Native image/door/light validators still apply. Presence rectangles rotate only in multiples of 90 degrees; incompatible geometry fails the command rather than approximating it. Torch images keep their linked light/effects together. These are immediate transforms, without animation, and do not change a mechanism's state by themselves. Transforms change live native geometry, preserving the editable source. Linked ownership records recognize authorized Blueprint transforms, so they alone do not cause a manual-edit conflict. Update scene reapplies authored positions and angles; unrelated manual edits retain their existing conflict protection. Set interaction controls direct player activation of a door, lever or torch, including the torch's flame button. The source default is enabled; the authored setting is available in Selection. Disabled controls cannot be activated by pointer or keyboard, and the server refuses forged direct requests. GMs retain manual override. This gate does not stop authored automation, signals or timers; normal action permissions and lock rules still apply. A live interaction flag survives a linked update while its authored default is unchanged; changing the authored default applies the new setting. It also survives reconnect and archives. Set region changes presence detection. Disabling quietly clears occupancy; enabling establishes a fresh baseline without synthetic entry/exit events. Signals and scheduled work keep their normal lifecycle. Moving or rotating a region also establishes a quiet baseline. Use later token commands for new presence events. Trigger context Event context supplies one typed Value selected by Context field : Property Value --- --- Event Text identifying the graph currently running Triggering element ID / user ID / user name Original source element and authenticated command actor Triggering token ID / actor ID Original presence token and its actor, or empty text without a token Presence transition / Occupancy count Original entry/exit transition and count after that transition; empty text/0 otherwise Has triggering token Boolean suitable for a Condition's Test input Current state / Previous state State values for this graph's event snapshot Connect identity text to Compare value or Switch, count to numeric comparisons, or Has triggering token directly to Test. Trigger metadata comes from validated server objects. Signals, Delay and Timer keep the original source, user and token metadata; they do not substitute the receiving element or the GM who inspected the queue. Event/state/previous describe the event being evaluated. Delay retains its original event snapshot; a Timer expiry takes fresh state/variable snapshots while keeping original trigger identity. No arbitrary signal payload is accepted. Simulation context fields are temporary preview values. Simulation lists group actions and context reads without moving game objects, changing flags, storing progress or running receiving graphs. These nodes require Blueprint version 2. Switch and weighted Random Add node → Logic → Switch selects one path by a Boolean, number or text Value . A connected Value replaces the configured Default value ; without a connection, that fallback is used. Reads use the event's initial snapshot, like variable and condition nodes. Add one to four cases with distinct values of the selected type; Boolean cases are limited to False and True. Equality does not convert values: text 1 and number 1 are different types, and text comparison is case-sensitive. False, zero and empty text remain valid values. The matching Case output runs; Default runs when none matches. Case IDs remain stable when another case is removed, preserving the remaining wires. Removing a case also removes its wires. Changing the value type resets the fallback and case values, removes incompatible Value wires and any discarded case outputs (at most two remain for Boolean). Each edit can be undone with its previous values and connections. An unconnected selected output ends that path; it does not fall through to Default. The editor makes room around expanded choice cards using their rendered size, including translated text. Layout changes caused by editing save with the graph and can be undone. Opening an unchanged graph preserves its saved coordinates. Add node → Logic → Random has two to four Branch outputs. Each weight is an integer from 0 to 1,000, and at least one must be positive. For example, weights 1 and 3 give 25% and 75% chances. Zero disables that branch. The draw includes every configured branch, even if it has no wire; an unconnected chosen branch ends the path without drawing again. Adding or removing the last branch updates its output, and Undo restores its wires. A shared choice node runs once when execution branches reconverge within the same event. Both nodes require Blueprint version 2. The GM automation log shows the selected case and typed input, or selected random branch and weight. Random is selected on the server under the same permissions, transactions and operation receipts as other actions. Retrying the same logical operation preserves its draw, including after a failed transaction; it cannot reroll by repeating that request. Delay continuations preserve choices already made, and Delay/Timer chains carry the private draw sequence forward without resetting it. These nodes add no persistent gate-memory entry. Saved projects, native copies and campaign archives preserve authored fallbacks and case values as content, including UUID-like text. Simulate highlights one selected path. Random draws locally for the preview; the game makes its own choice. Neither simulation writes scene state nor runs signal receivers or scheduled work. Persistent execution controls Add node → Logic includes Counter , Once and Cooldown . Each has one execution Input and two execution branches; these nodes do not expose value outputs. Their private progress belongs to this element and is identified by the event and node ID. Two nodes or two receiving graphs keep separate progress, even when they have the same configuration. Node Behavior --- --- Counter Increment once per event visit, then choose Reached when the count is at least the Activation target ; otherwise choose Below target . The target is an integer from 1 to 1,000,000. Count saturates at 1,000,000, and Reached stays active on later visits. Once Choose First time once, then Already used until the GM resets this node. Place it before the effects it protects. Cooldown Choose Ready on the first visit or after its deadline; otherwise choose Cooling down . Cooldown seconds accepts 0.1–86,400 seconds. Blocked attempts keep the existing deadline. For three activations followed by one reward, connect the event to Counter with target 3, Reached → Once , then First time → Change state → Play sound . Counting activations of one element differs from checking the current states of three distinct torches with All/Any. Shared controls execute once when branches reconverge during one event, like other execution nodes. Cooldown uses the server's UTC clock and persists an absolute deadline. Elapsing time does not run a graph: another authorized event must visit the node. Each execution segment commits progress and effects together; a failed action rolls back that segment, and retrying the same operation does not consume another activation. Waiting uses the separate Delay node described below. The simulation's Persistent node preview fields configure the count before the event, whether Once was already used, and the seconds remaining for Cooldown. Each Simulate starts from those preview values and reports the selected branch; it does not read or change stored game progress. During play, the GM's Automation → Node memory view lists the stored controls. Reset node removes only that entry, checks the value shown to prevent stale resets, and runs no gameplay event. The next visit starts from the node's unused state. Players and streamers receive neither this memory nor private graph details. Reopening a scene, reconnecting, server restart, linked builder updates and campaign archives preserve progress without replaying events. Native element copies start with empty control memory. Changing a target, duration, position or connection preserves existing progress; a changed duration applies after the current deadline next permits activation. Removing a node/event or changing its type discards that entry. These controls require Blueprint version 2. Persistent Delay Add node → Logic → Delay uses Wait seconds (default 3), from 0.1 to 86,400 seconds, before continuing from Next . For example: Lever turned → Change state: Open → Delay: 3 seconds → Change state: Closed . Delay requires Blueprint version 2. A reached Delay suspends the rest of this event, including later Sequence branches, preserving their execution order. Actions before the wait commit together with its saved continuation. Other interactions can still run while this event waits. The continuation resumes on the server without repeating the event or earlier actions. Closing the editor, disconnecting every browser or restarting the server does not discard it; overdue work runs when the server is available. No database transaction remains open during the wait. State, previous state, referenced element states and variable reads retain the snapshot taken when this event began, including values first read after the wait. Set variable actions already committed before the wait affect later events; reads in this event keep its original snapshot. Counter, Once and Cooldown consult their current stored progress when execution resumes. Automation → Waiting shows the GM each pending wait, its element, event, actor and due time. Cancel wait removes the remaining continuation without undoing effects already committed or firing another event. Cancellation checks the displayed due time and requires a refresh if the wait changed. Pausing scene automation keeps pending waits, including overdue ones, until Resume automation . Leaving or hiding a scene does not itself pause its automation. Changing the owning blueprint's behavior, connections or duration cancels its pending continuation; moving graph cards alone preserves it. Removing the owner or an element target used by the continuation cancels the wait. Missing light, sound or image bindings anywhere in the owning blueprint also cancel it, including resources used only before the wait. At resume, the server checks the original actor's current membership and access again; later promotion grants no extra authority to a player-started wait. A resumed segment that fails commits none of its effects and records a diagnostic, while effects committed before the wait remain. Delay and Timer share a queue of 64 pending jobs per scene and 256 per campaign. A root chain keeps its existing limits across waits: 32 element operations, 256 scene-signal deliveries, four operations per element and 1,024 actions, plus at most 32 timed resumptions. Resuming a Delay continuation does not consume another element-operation slot. Pending continuations are private runtime work; campaign exports, snapshots and copies do not carry them. Simulate stops at the first reached Delay, highlights that wait and reports its duration. The preview never advances time, schedules work or runs the continuation. Use an actual scene to verify delayed effects. Persistent Timer Add node → Logic → Timer controls a named, one-shot countdown. Its Name uses the same case-sensitive ASCII format as a signal: 1–64 characters, starting with a letter, then letters, digits, underscores, dots or hyphens. The name belongs to this element; several nodes or events on that element can control the same countdown. A timer has no Target input and does not address another element or the whole scene. Action Behavior --- --- Start timer Create the countdown if it is absent. If it is already pending, preserve its identity, deadline, original actor and execution budget. Stop timer Cancel the matching pending countdown without firing its event. Stopping an absent timer has no effect. Restart timer Replace the countdown and start a new one from now, using this event's actor and execution budget. It also starts an absent timer. Start and Restart use Timer seconds , from 0.1 to 86,400 seconds (default 3). Stop has no duration. Next runs immediately for every action; the timer does not suspend the sending event. To close a door later, create On signal → CloseLater , connect that receiver to Change state: Closed , then start a Timer named CloseLater from the interaction. Other connected actions can run immediately while that countdown is pending. At expiry the server sends signal:CloseLater only to its owning element. This is a fresh event: state, referenced states and variable reads use the values at expiry, while Counter, Once and Cooldown use their current stored progress. It does not repeat the event that started the timer. Without a matching receiving graph, the timer completes without effects; the editor shows a hint to add one. Timer requires Blueprint version 2. It has no repeating mode or global trigger. Automation → Waiting identifies each Timer by name, owning element, actor and expiry time. The GM can use Stop timer , or Restart timer to count again from now using the saved duration. Both check the displayed identity and deadline; stale requests require refresh. A GM restart preserves the original actor, role ceiling and chain budget, so it cannot elevate a player-started timer. Neither control fires the expiry event immediately. The durable queue and server worker are shared with Delay. Timers survive closed browsers and server restart; scene pause keeps them pending until resume. Blueprint behavior changes, missing required targets/resources and loss of access cancel them under the same policy as Delay; moving graph cards or renaming the map preserves them. At expiry the original actor's current access is checked again. Effects, completion and the receipt commit together; failure rolls back that expiry's effects and records a diagnostic. Earlier committed effects remain. Timers and Delays share the 64-per-scene/256-per-campaign pending limits and the original chain's 32 timed resumptions, 32 element operations, 256 scene-signal deliveries, four operations per element and 1,024 actions. A Timer expiry consumes a new element operation; a Delay continuation does not. Rearming from a receiving graph keeps those limits, so this is not an unbounded repeating scheduler. Running timers are private work and do not enter campaign exports, snapshots or copies. Simulate lists timer actions and follows Next, without starting a countdown, advancing time or executing its receiver. Select the named signal graph to simulate that receiver separately, and use a real scene to verify expiry. Test behavior through the server Choose Test behavior in the Builder to rehearse the current unsaved document. The selected starting event runs against the current configuration without an implicit comparison. The result shows the element's state before the event and after the test settles, including presence changes caused by a teleport or move. Each changed element is listed by name with readable facts, such as a door going from Closed to Opened , a region going from Occupied to Empty with the token that left, or a teleport naming the token, destination and cell. Raw stored values remain under a collapsed Technical details entry. Select an element, one of its defined events and, optionally, a Test actor . The server builds a temporary native scene and runs the real engine, including cross-element actions, signals, variables, native effects and token transport. The preview applies the returned changes to a separate copy of the map. It does not change the source, selection history or saved project. No generation, image rendering or new media files are needed. In the table's Automation → Elements panel, Test behavior rehearses the selected live element against the current scene. An optional Test token must belong to that scene; its actor and identity come from the server. In a Builder draft, the selected campaign actor supplies an ephemeral token, centered in the selected region when applicable. Tests run with the GM's permissions. They do not impersonate a player or replace checking a player's actual permissions. Run test shows the executed events and steps, predicted state changes, variables, audio changes and token destinations. Every run starts from the current configuration. Reset test clears the temporary result; closing the window also discards the preview. Tests always roll back scene objects, tokens, variables, node memory, jobs, logs and revisions. They create no receipts and deliver no sounds, messages, handouts, camera moves or realtime notifications. A failed chain shows its diagnostic and predicts no committed partial effects. Delay stops traversal at the wait, and Timer actions are listed with their predicted scheduling changes. Time does not advance and scheduled receivers do not fire. Without a test actor/token, Teleport is explicitly skipped with a warning while later actions continue. A paused scene can be rehearsed without changing its pause flag. Simulate remains available in the graph editor for the existing local graph-only preview. Automation log during play On the table, the GM's Walls layer has an Automation tool that opens a floating window with the current scene's recent door blueprint runs, newest first. Each run shows its outcome ( Completed , Blocked by the lock or Failed ), time, who acted, the state before and after, and every executed event with its nodes in order: the branch each condition took, the values read and the actions with their parameters. A failure also shows its reason, such as a refused player or disabled dynamic lighting, and keeps the steps reached before it; none of its effects persist. Problems hides completed runs, and the crosshair pings the door on the map without broadcasting the ping. The window updates as runs happen and closes with Escape . Elements provides searchable, type-filtered controls for doors, levers, torches, regions, native images and dynamic surfaces. Select an element to locate it, edit its behavior or test it. Controls apply immediately to the live scene: open/close/lock a door, toggle a mechanism or flame, show/hide artwork, enable player interaction or enable a region. Dynamic surfaces also offer a material choice and Restore original appearance , preserving their generated base image, mask and collision. Hiding a torch also gates its owned light and effects; its mechanism and flame remain independent. Lights, particle emitters and shaders appear in the same panel, with their own type filters. Edit settings opens their existing native editor; changes apply only when saved, and Cancel preserves the scene. Their enabled switches use the same authorized native commands and revision checks. Remote updates refresh the panel while preserving a material selected before Apply material . Selecting a door state changes it directly without starting a graph. Run interaction starts onInteract ; state and image changes require action nodes. An empty blueprint does not toggle a lever or torch. Region changes establish occupancy quietly, without inventing arrival/departure events. These are GM controls: player interaction flags do not block the GM. Commands check the displayed object revision and use receipts for retries; a conflict requires a refresh. They preserve the authored Builder document. Existing variable and node memory resets keep their expected-value checks in their respective panels. Pause automation stops every element graph in the scene. Interacting with a blueprint does not change its state or execute actions, and the log records Automation paused . Objects without a blueprint retain their native controls; direct GM configuration remains available. Players lose the interaction exception at locked doors. Resume automation restores the graphs. Only GMs can pause, run or clear; the paused flag is kept in the scene settings. Runs are diagnostics, not campaign content. The server records them in the same transaction as the door operation, or after the rollback for a failure; a retry of the same request returns its receipt without another run. Each scene keeps its last 50 runs, and archives do not export them. Only GMs can read them through GET /api/maps/<scene_id /automation or receive the maps.automation socket notice; players and streamers receive neither. Levers Place an Object with an image classified as Object , select it and open Panels → Selection . Set Behavior → Lever and choose its Initial state : Deactivated or Activated . An image is required for this artwork-based lever; choose Empty Object for an image-free controller. Setting Behavior back to None removes its behavior and graphs; project undo restores them. Double-click the lever or choose Edit behavior to open Smart object . Its main ports are On interaction and On destroy ; use Check state inside the graph to choose between Activated and Deactivated, then add the state and image actions to each branch. Configure native appearance, a hidden image or another Object image independently for each state. Changing images preserves the authored box and rotation. Initial-state and geometry edits configure the project without executing gameplay events. Element reference can select a door or lever by list or Pick on map . Change state offers the target's supported states; doors and levers can control each other. The activation branch of On interaction can continue through Change state: Activated → Change state: Opened , with a door reference in the last action's Target . Enable Players may lock or unlock when this action must unlock that door for a player. Get property and Compare state can also read a referenced lever. Reveal and Set barrier apply to doors; unsupported actions are skipped with a diagnostic in Automation . Copying a group remaps references between its copied doors, levers and lights, preserving references outside the group. On the generated game scene, choose Select and the Game layer, then double-click the visible lever to run its interaction. The GM can also interact on the GM layer. A single click selects it; double-clicking in the Map Builder opens its behavior editor instead. The interaction toggles the state when its graph requests that change. An empty blueprint does not toggle; a mechanism without a blueprint retains native interaction. Streamers remain read-only. Players receive only its current state and active image. Automation lists doors and levers together; pausing automation stops graph execution. Scene updates preserve its live state. Direct shader controls In a Smart Object Blueprint, add Control shader , choose a shader from the same map and select its property. The action supports enabled state, color, intensity, opacity, speed, scale, radius, rotation, light response and emission. Connect an interaction, area event, signal or another action to its execution input. Chain several nodes to change multiple properties. The Value input accepts a Boolean, Text or Number connection according to the selected property; color uses a six-digit hex value. Native shader limits also apply to connected values. Independent shaders and composed torch shaders are supported. A component's enabled setting is retained while its torch is extinguished or hidden and is restored when the flame becomes visible. The action can update its parameters while the flame is off. Existing Set light and Set flame actions remain available. Shader targets follow copied objects and generated scene IDs, and can be rebound in saved behavior templates. Rehearsals report the changed shader without persisting the test. Updating an unchanged Builder parameter preserves its live value; an explicit Builder edit replaces that parameter. Composed torches Place an Object image, select it and choose Behavior → Torch in Panels → Selection . The builder creates a linked native light; Torch components can add particles and a shader. Edit opens the game's own window for each component while keeping the torch selected. Components share the image's project layer and each belongs to exactly one torch. Mechanism → Normal/Turned and Flame lit are independent. Turned adds 90 degrees to the authored orientation around the image's center, carrying its components. Extinguishing the flame disables light and effects without moving the mechanism; lighting it restores only components configured as enabled. Positions, radii and other native settings remain editable. A state appearance with a hidden image also hides the components' emission. Moving, rotating, resizing or changing the torch's layer carries its components. Builder duplication creates independent components and remaps internal Blueprint references. Each operation supports undo. Deleting the torch deletes its components; deleting an optional effect only detaches that effect. Deleting its required light dissolves the composition, preserving the image and removing its remaining components. Removing the behavior also preserves the image. Double-click or choose Edit behavior to open the torch's Blueprint. Connect On interaction → Check state: Normal → True → Change state: Turned → Change state: Opened , with a door reference in the last action's Target , to turn the torch and open a passage. Add its image and other effects in the same branch. Set flame lights/extinguishes this torch or a torch connected to Target , preserving its mechanism; doors and levers can also use this node. Builder configuration edits do not execute gameplay events. In the game scene, choose Select and the Game layer, then double-click the visible image to run its interaction and turn or return the mechanism when configured to do so. The GM can also interact on the GM layer. In the Map Builder, double-click opens the behavior editor. Its flame action appears on pointer hover or keyboard focus; Enter/Space activate focused controls. Streamers remain read-only. Players receive only the active image, mechanism and flame; private links and graphs remain GM-only. Automation includes torches and their actions. Save/reopen, generation, updates and campaign archives preserve the composition. Updating the scene preserves live mechanism and flame state; incompatible manual edits to native objects cause the normal conflict without silent replacement. Regions and pressure plates In Panels → Tools , choose Region and drag a rectangle over the map. Use Selection to name it, resize it, choose its layer, enable presence triggers or restrict its elevation range. The rectangle is a GM guide; it is absent from the raster, builder preview and player scene projection. For a pressure plate, choose a Controlled door and Apply pressure plate . This explicitly replaces the region's Blueprint: the first token opens the door and the last token leaving closes it. With two tokens inside, removing only one does not release the plate. Edit behavior and double-click open the normal Blueprint editor for custom sound, light, torch and door actions. Regions have derived Empty and Occupied states. On area enter and On area exit start a sequence for every eligible token crossing the boundary; these events do not compare state or occupant count. Use Event context → Occupancy count and a comparison node for first-entry ( 1 ) or last-exit ( 0 ) actions. Region state cannot be set manually or changed by a Change state node. The server evaluates the token's center and elevation along its validated path. A segment crossing the entire rectangle enters and exits it; a preview drag does not run automation. Overlapping regions evaluate independently in creation order. Token placement, duplication, removal and elevation changes also update presence. Hidden tokens still occupy space; their IDs remain private. Blocked moves and failed actions roll back the whole command, and retries do not repeat effects. Actions retain the moving user's existing permissions, including locked-door restrictions. Reopening a scene does not replay entry events. Editing or enabling a region, or updating its linked scene, establishes current occupancy without synthetic entry events. Changing configuration therefore does not automatically operate the linked door. The native GM region editor shows state and occupant count; the Automation window records the actual instigating token for each run. Source documents and scenes allow up to 128 presence areas in total: regions plus objects with connected area-event graphs. They also count in the normal object limit. Presence filters in Selection and the native region editor can restrict token IDs, actor IDs, disposition ( Friendly , Neutral , Hostile , Unknown ) and visibility ( Any , Visible , Hidden ). Each identity list accepts up to 64 unique IDs. Empty lists impose no restriction. Members within one list use OR; different criteria use AND. Visibility checks the token's hidden setting, not a participant's fog-of-war view or control permissions. Hidden tokens remain eligible when no visibility filter excludes them. Only matching tokens count as occupants or fire presence events. Editing filters, geometry or enabled state quietly recomputes occupancy; later authoritative token commands generate new transitions. Existing projects with no filters retain their previous behavior. Filters and occupancy remain private to GMs; actor/token ownership and scene/campaign boundaries are validated on the server. Use Event context to inspect the triggering token/actor and original count, or Set region to change presence detection from a graph. Same-scene Teleport uses that verified trigger token; it does not use the browser's current selection. Reusable behavior templates The Smart Object editor's template library belongs to the campaign and is available only to GMs. Saving a template captures an independent snapshot of the behavior. Typed resource positions become named bindings for images, elements, lights, sounds, handouts and participants; Self bindings resolve to the receiving instance. Choose scalar parameters to expose, such as a duration, volume, flag or message. Authored text, signal names, variable values and graph/node identities keep their meaning, including text that resembles a resource UUID. Applying a template asks for its bindings and parameter values, then creates an independent draft in the current editor. Review bindings before applying; valid applied changes save automatically through the project or scene-network flow. Changing the library entry later does not update existing instances. Missing or incompatible bindings must be resolved; a template does not grant access to another campaign's resources. Campaign archives preserve the library and its typed definition without retaining another instance's private resource identities. Scene network Open Scene network from the GM's Automation window to inspect the scene's element-owned rules, references and missing bindings. Doors, levers, torches and presence regions open their existing Smart Object editor; ordinary images and dynamic surfaces can be targets without acquiring an invented mechanism state. Generated internal composition planes are not offered as editable elements. Saving checks both the native object's revision and the linked project's revision. For a generated element, the native blueprint, authored source blueprint and that blueprint's ownership snapshot update in one transaction. Typed native targets are mapped back to source identities; authored labels and text remain unchanged. Standalone native elements save only their native definition. Viewing the network creates no second graph store or additional execution. A conflict requires refresh; the operation never adopts unrelated manual geometry changes. Reusing a request UUID with another payload is rejected. Control progress clocks Create a progress clock (clocks.md) on the table or in campaign management, then choose Add node → Actions → Control clock in the Smart Object editor. Select the clock, choose an action and connect an event or another action to Input . Connect Next to continue the sequence after the clock operation. Action Effect --- --- Advance clock Add Amount to the current progress Reduce clock Subtract Amount from the current progress Set clock value Set progress to Amount Reset clock Return progress to zero; Amount is ignored Amount is an integer from 0 to 24. Progress stays between zero and the clock's segment count. A numeric Amount input replaces the saved fallback amount; for example, connect a number from Get variable . The fallback control is disabled while that input is connected, and Reset disables it independently. The saved version-2 action is clockControl with clockId , action ( advance , reduce , set or reset ) and integer amount . Clock names remain authored text. Targets must belong to the campaign and have campaign scope or belong to the executing scene. Existing clocks from another scene or campaign cannot be bound. A missing or unavailable clock produces a diagnostic and refuses the operation without committing partial effects. Generate creates a new scene. A clock scoped to the linked scene can be saved, rehearsed and used by Update scene , but cannot be carried into a different newly generated scene. Use a campaign clock or review and rebind the target for the destination scene; generation never changes a clock's scope. A GM-authored binding delegates that specific operation to the mechanism. A player allowed to interact with it can trigger the operation even when the clock is private or direct player editing is disabled. This grants no general clock controls or access to private clock names, values or graphs. The runtime requires an active campaign GM and retains the map command's transaction, revision, retry and post-commit notification rules. Simulate lists the planned clock actions without changing saved progress. Test behavior uses the real server engine, shows each clock's before/after progress, and rolls back clock rows and receipts with the rest of the rehearsal. Committed play updates the same clock window and permitted pinned HUD; opening the node editor or running a preview preserves saved progress. Control clues Prepare a clue (clues.md) on the table or in campaign management, then choose Add node → Actions → Control clue . Select the clue and connect the event to Input . Connect Next to continue after the operation. There is no Target port: the GM chooses the specific clue in the node. Action Result --- --- Advance clue Add Amount to progress Reduce clue Subtract Amount from progress Set clue progress Set progress to Amount Reset clue Return progress to zero Reveal clue Complete progress and set visibility to Players Hide clue Set visibility to GM only, preserving progress Amount is an integer from 0 to 24. A connected numeric Amount overrides the configured amount, and progress is bounded by the clue's segment count. Reset, reveal and hide ignore Amount. The saved version-2 node is clueControl , with clueId , action ( advance , reduce , set , reset , reveal or hide ) and integer amount . Players see a finding only when its progress is complete and its visibility is Players. The server omits undiscovered records and all GM notes from player and streamer projections. A player can trigger a GM-authored mechanism's specific clue operation without receiving general clue editing permission. Execution requires an active campaign GM and validates the clue's campaign and scene scope. Campaign clues can accompany a newly generated scene. A clue scoped to a linked scene can be saved, tested and used when updating that scene, but Generate creates a different scene. Rebind the target or use a campaign clue for the new scene; generation does not change the clue's scope. Simulate preserves saved progress. Test behavior previews changes through the real server engine and rolls back clue records, receipts and notifications. Normal committed interactions update the shared clue panel and permitted pinned display. Reducing progress below completion, resetting or hiding a clue removes it from current player views. Open and control mind maps Prepare a mind map (mindmaps.md) on the table or in campaign management, then choose Open mind map or Control mind-map topic under Add node → Actions . Connect the event to Input and Next to the following action. Select the map and, for a completion action, its topic. Opening can optionally focus a topic. The version-2 openMindMap node stores mindMapId , nodeId (or null ) and audience . Audience uses {scope:"trigger"} , {scope:"players"} , or {scope:"users", userIds: ... } . Each recipient must retain read access to the map and its scene. The mindMapNode node stores mindMapId , nodeId and action: "complete" "reset" "toggle" ; it changes that topic's Boolean completion through the native service. Bindings use campaign maps or maps scoped to the executing scene. A GM-authored completion binding delegates only that operation, requires an active campaign GM and grants no general graph editing rights. Deleted targets remain in the graph for repair and fail safely if executed. Delayed work rechecks its bindings. Simulate describes the action; Test behavior runs the server engine and rolls back graph changes, receipts and notifications. Generated/updated scenes retain these bindings, and campaign copies remap their typed targets. Dynamic surfaces Select a floor or wall and enable Dynamic surface before generating/updating the scene. Existing projects keep their static default. Generated dynamic artwork uses native image planes and bounded masks instead of retaining the same pixels in the background raster. Paint, transparency, holes, erasers, wall crop and texture phase preserve their composition; internal planes and generated assets stay out of the ordinary asset/target catalogs. Set visibility ( setVisibility , visible ) and Set appearance ( setAppearance , assetId ) accept Self or a connected element/group Target. Dynamic surfaces change their visible layer or material without rebaking the map or writing runtime files. Ordinary live images and door/lever/torch artwork also support the compatible visual action. Stateful artwork follows its existing sprite and state-entry lifecycle. These actions change artwork; use the separate Barrier action when collision, vision, light or sound blocking should change too. Only ordinary campaign images can become materials; generated masks and composite artwork cannot be reused as source assets. Explicit source updates keep the documented ownership and manual-conflict checks. Messages, handouts and camera focus Version 2 provides Show message , Show handout and Camera focus : Node Saved settings --- --- showMessage text with 1–2,000 nonblank characters and audience showHandout Existing campaign journalId and audience cameraFocus focusX and focusY in cells, each 0–1,000, and audience Audience is the authenticated triggering participant, the campaign's players, or an explicit list of 1–64 unique participants. The server validates current membership and scene access for each recipient. Handouts open the existing journal window only for recipients who already have read access; presentation creates no permanent or temporary grant. Messages display plain text. Delivery occurs after commit, with one presentation identity for client deduplication; rollback and receipt replay do not repeat it. Camera coordinates are separate from the node's layout x/y . The server converts cells to scene pixels and rejects points outside the map. Camera requests apply only to the recipient's current scene and respect Preferences → Allow automation camera focus , which is off by default and stored per profile/device. Messages and authorized handouts can be shown while another scene is being viewed. None of these actions changes the campaign's broadcast scene. Same-scene teleport Connect a region's On area enter event to Teleport and select a destination presence region in the same scene. The saved node is teleport: { destinationId: <region UUID } ; token and actor identities come only from the authenticated Event Context. Browser selection and payload token IDs cannot replace the traveler. Direct interactions with no triggering token cannot teleport. The server rechecks current scene access, actor identity/control, token lock and revision, destination activation/elevation, map bounds and footprint capacity. It chooses the first free integer-grid placement inside the destination, scanning rows from top to bottom and columns from left to right. Other tokens, including hidden ones, and walls through the destination footprint block placement; walls along the skipped route do not. Search work is bounded. An invalid or full destination fails the current transaction and leaves the original token unchanged. The same token retains its actor, linked/snapshot data, conditions, ownership and settings. Its placement and revisions commit with the logical command receipt. On the tabletop, teleport removes the token's old visual object and creates it at the destination without animating the skipped distance. The token keeps its identity and selection; duplicate acknowledgements do not repeat the visual replacement. The camera and floor stay mounted. Departure and arrival run once, without firing regions merely crossed by the teleport line. Arrival can run sound, light and appearance actions. A private, persisted arrival gate blocks an automatic onward/return teleport from that region until the token leaves; re-entering enables that route again. One token can be teleported at most once per logical command, including overlapping regions and signals. Gates survive reconnects, waits and compatible scene updates and are never included in participant projections. Delay/Timer retain the original token/actor identity and role ceiling, then recheck current control and destination when resuming. A reassigned actor or revoked access cannot redirect that identity. Effects committed before a wait retain their usual semantics if the later segment fails. Cross-scene transfer (8B), group travel and participant-following/navigation policies (8C) remain future work; this action never changes scene selection or broadcast. Current limitations Smart Objects cover doors, levers, torches and presence regions; references also reach ordinary live images, native lights and campaign sounds. Typed groups are explicit ordered lists. Value wires include their resource/set types alongside State, True or False, Number and Text. Get property still exposes only current or previous state; Event context supplies trusted trigger metadata. Named signals carry no custom payload, and simulation previews one graph at a time. The editor has no comments, visual node groups, reroutes or node bypass, and its undo history ends with the modal. The automation log keeps 50 runs per scene for elements with a blueprint. Direct interaction runs apply to doors, levers and torches; region events require authoritative token commands. See Current limitations and pending work (smart-objects-direction.md current-limitations-and-pending-work) for the full list and the next steps. Developer reference The sections below describe stored documents, native projections, HTTP commands and execution boundaries. For user operations, use the workflows above. The frontend guide (frontend.md map-builder-workspace) maps controllers and generated assets; the testing guide (testing.md) documents isolated regression scenarios. Source, raster and live geometry MapBuilderProject belongs to one campaign and contains its folder, versioned JSON source, last generated scene reference and generation ownership history. Project endpoints recheck GM membership on every request. They do not expose drafts to players or streamers. Campaign exports, clones and snapshots preserve projects and remap references to uploaded assets. Exporting the latest generated scene as content includes its editable project. Clones remap native light, image and sound references while preserving authored source identities. When audio is excluded from a campaign export, its exported source, native objects and ownership history omit legacy sound action nodes and reconnect their continuations. Other blueprint actions remain intact; the original campaign is unchanged. Schema version 3 stores name , columns , rows , cellSize , background , and the assets , layers , floors , walls , doors , decorations and lights lists, plus optional particles , shaders and regions lists. Older version-3 documents can omit those lists without changing on read. An empty layers list is valid only when every object list is empty; saving or generating it adds no default layer. Every object references an existing layerId ; layers contain id , name , visible and locked . Floors support 0/90/180/270-degree texture rotation. Optional backgroundImage: {assetId} references one campaign image independently of brush assets and stretches it beneath the authored layers. Decorations contain a bounding box and rotation; their images use contain-fit. An Empty Object is a decoration with empty: true , assetId: null , optional name , and a native lever: {state: "off" "on"} . Its optional blueprint uses kind: "lever" , all default state appearances inherit, and image actions cannot target the owner. Lights contain cell-space coordinates and bright/dim radii plus native light settings. Particle and shader entries use native property names and validation, plus id and layerId . Their x/y use project cells and become native pixels; light radii and shader radius remain cells ( radius: 0 covers the scene). Shader names and source remain authored content through campaign cloning and archives; object identities and ownership references still remap. Region entries contain id , layerId , name , enabled , the cell-space rectangle x/y/width/height , optional vertical: {bottom, top} and optional version-2 blueprint with kind: "region" . Their states are empty and occupied ; graphs also accept presence:enter and presence:exit . Optional filters: {tokenIds, actorIds, dispositions, visibility} stores authored selectors; computed occupancy and its token-membership ledger remain runtime-only. Generation uses stable native zones IDs, remaps Blueprint references and keeps regions GM-only. Walls and doors may additionally store native presentation , behavior: {movement, vision, light, sound} , vertical: {bottom, top} and discovered . Elevation values retain the game's token-elevation units; bottom/top: null means no elevation limit. Generation flattens behavior and elevation into the native wall fields. Older objects that omit these settings retain their existing defaults without a source rewrite. Optional Boolean artwork on walls and doors defaults to true. False retains the barrier while omitting its painted artwork; imported collision geometry uses this flag. An independent collision wall retains its native ID when moved. Version-three documents may store sceneGeometry: {width, height, gridSize, gridOffsetX, gridOffsetY, imageScale} . Width/height are exact positive pixel integers; the grid retains native numeric sizes/offsets and image scale (optional, default 1). Integer columns/rows describe a containing workspace; raster output and the base image use the exact dimensions. Changing workspace dimensions or cell size clears this imported geometry. POST /api/containers/{campaign}/map-builder/scenes/{scene}/adopt accepts {request_id, expected_scene_version} and returns {project, scene, warnings} . It checks GM membership and scene ownership, serializes project creation under the campaign lock, reuses existing links and records a retry receipt. Storage created by a failed adoption is removed. The source manifest records precisely which original native objects the project owns; subsequent updates preserve external content and the normal revision/conflict checks. Synchronization also imports native grid calibration without moving objects.
